summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68. The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,23,994/ as the net wealth of the assessee on the outstandings of the money lending business. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner followed the view taken by the Income Tax Officer. In appeal to this Court it was contended that accrued interest was liable to be included in the wealth tax assessments and that the High Court erred in holding that accrued interests were liable to he included in wealth tax assessment. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The computation of the net assets of an assessee call for a determination of his assets and debts as on the valuation date. [310C] 2. The scheme of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957, the net value of an asset which is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of s.7 as the estimated price, which, in the opinion of the wealth Tax Officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the Valuation date. It is apparent that what accrues as a right also falls to be excluded within the assets of the asses see under the Wealth tax Act. That being so, the conclusion is inescapable that even though the accounts of the assesses are maintained on cash basis interest due on accrual basis, although not realised, on the Outstandings, of the moneys lending business are liable to been included in its net wealth. [309F G] 3. The principle of apportionment of the assets amongst the assessee has to be taken into account and it is immaterial whether the assessee employs one system of accounting or another. There is clear indication that the assets to be considered are not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of accountancy adopted by the assessee. [311G H] 4. The concept of "net wealth" which speaks of "the aggregate value" of all the assets belonging to the assessee, on valuation date, is in excess of the aggregate value of all those assets belonging by the assesseee on the date of valuation. All the assets, of a assessee, bar those expressly excepted by the statute, are to be treated as covered by the assets. [312A B] 5. The principles of apportionment laid down by the Supreme Court in Vedrevu Venkappa Rao (supra) and in Commissioner of Wealth Tax, A.P. I vs Kavigolla Narasimha Rao (Orissa) (AIR 1977 SC 853) are applicable to the instant case. [313C D] 6. The assessee is entitled to claim deduction under section 27(1)(c) of the Act on account of interest received by him on accrual of interest on accrual ground. [317D] 7. The expression "net assets" which speak of "accrue interest" must be read in its ordinary sense and not in its popular sense. [320F] 8. The term "net asset" is used in the context of the statute or the Act, as the case may be. It has to receive a meaning which will have regard to all the relevant provisions of the Income tax Act including the Wealth Act. [322G H; 320A] 9. The expressions "net value" and "net amount" are not defined in the Wealth (Tax) Act. They are used in different senses, but they are not intended to be understood in their popular sense as understood in common parlance. [323H; 322A B]. 10. The word "net" is not defined either in the Income (tax) Act or in the Indian Income Tax Act. It does not mean that all assets which are expressly excepted from the operation of the provisions of Wealth tax Acts should be taken to have been included within the net Wealth of the assessees. The respondent was a workman in the appellant company. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had committed misconduct and was not found guilty of any misconduct. The respondent filed an application before the Central Administrative Tribunal for setting aside the order of dismissal. The Tribunal held that the punishment of dismissal should be maintained but set aside the penalty imposed by the disciplinary authority. The appellant company preferred a writ petition in this Court challenging the order passed by the Tribu nal on the grounds that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the penalty if the conclusion of the Inquiry Officer or the Tribunal was based on evidence even if some of it is found to be irrelevant or extraneous to the matter. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court has no juris diction under Article 226 of the Constitution to interfere in a case where the Tribunal is satisfied that if some but not all of t he findings of the Tribunal were "unreasonable", the order cannot be sustained. [27F] 2.1 In the instant case, the Tribunal imposed a lesser penalty on the respond ent. The Court has not gone into the question whether the punishment imposed by th e disciplinary authority can be supported on any finding as to substantial misdemeanour for which the punishment can lawfully be imposed, it is not for the Court to consider whether that ground alone would have weighed with the authority in imposing the punishment. [28F] 3.2 The Tribunal has no jurisdiction if the findings of t his Inquiry Officer are based on the evidence even though some of them may be found to he irrelevant or irrelevant. If the inference that the penalty of dismissal from service imposed upon the appellant was too seve rred, it was not for thority to consider any finding on substantial misdemeanor for which t he punishment could lawfully be impose, it has no merits. [29F] 4. The order of the Tribun al imposing a lesser punishment on the appel lant cannot, therefore, be sustained.[30A B] 5. In Shankar Dass vs Union of India this Court set aside t he impugned order of penalty on t he ground that the imposition of the penalty was too harsh to the responde nt. [31F G] 6. The question whether a punishment of dismissing from service passed by an authority can he supported on some finding as regards substantial misdemeano f for which no penalty can lawfully been imposed, is not deter mined in this case since the respondent had already retired from service and his reinstatement in service was not challenged. [32F G; 33A] 7. The res pondent has failed to establish any misconduct or negligence on his part. If it is his case that he was not in fact the person convicted, it would be open to him to challenge the finding of the inquiry officer or the Tribuna nal. [33G H] 8. In the light of the principles to which we have call ed attention and in view of the aforesaid discussion, the ord er of the tribunal imposing a higher penalty on respondent cannot, however, be justified. [34F G].

The first ground on which the High Court dismissed the suit was that the suit for a declaration and injunction was barred by the principle of res judicata in view of the dismissal of the former suit No. 157 of 1968 filed by the appellants. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. It would be just and fair that the issue whether defendant No1 was a tenant or deemed tenant was not found in the former case and hence it could be argued that the second suit based on the factum of tenancy was not maintainable. [1032C] 2. The jurisdiction of civil court is specifically barred by section 58(2) of the Act. [1132D] 3. The petitioners are carpenters in the Government service. They have been working as daily rated employees. Their services were terminated by the Corporation on the ground that they had not completed 240 days of work in a year. The petitioners filed a writ petition before this Court challenging the termination of their services. This Court dismissed the petition holding that the petitioners are not entitled to any relief. In the appeal, it was contended for the Corporation that the unit where the petition ers were working is a factory registered under the Factories Act and the Government has not fixed the mini mum wages payable for similar work in the construction industry. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of "equal pay for equal work" is not one of the fundamental rights expressly guaranteed by our Constitution. There is no discrimination amongst the same set of employees by the same master in the same establishment. [667B] 2. The Corporation has no regularly employed carpenter nor it is a mere recent decision which has exhaustively dealt with all the principles bearing on the question of equal pay for Equal work in that principle. [668C D] 3. The Court held that the principle of 'equal pay ' for equal works cannot be invoked invariably in every kind of service particularly in the area of professional services. It is not permissible to provide two different pay scales in the similar cadre on the basis of selection based on merit with due regard to experience and seniority. [669D] 4. The principal claim of the petitioners therefore fails and is rejected. [670E F] 5. The court held that it is open to the State to classify employees on the same basis as the selection based upon merit with proper regard to competence and efficiency. [671F] 6. The principles of " equal pay" for equal Work cannot be enforced in every type of service especially in the areas of professional service. It has not been extended to employees of the Corporation. The petitioners have been treated as construction workers and they are being paid the minimum wages admissible to such workmen. [672F] 7. The writ petitions fail and are dismissed.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life by the Sessions Judge, Mehsana, in respect of murder of Malan and acquitted them. The High Court found that the prosecution had failed to prove the charge against accused 1 to 4 beyond reasonable doubt and acquitted all the accused except accused 5. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the evidence of PW 2, who had been tried along with accused 1, 6 and 7 was under section 34 read with Section 120B I. P.C., and that the conviction of accused 1 and 6 for the murder of the deceased was bad in law; (ii) the High Court erred in holding that the retracted judicial confession of accused 5 could not be relied upon against accused 2 because it had been recorded by the Magistrate under section 164 Cr. P C. The appellants contended that the evidence on record did not establish the charge of conspiracy under section 120B read with sections 120B and I.p.C.; (iii) the retracted Judicial confession of the accused 5 was not admissible in law as it was made before a Magistrate; (iv) the prosecution has failed to establish the case against accused 4 beyond any reasonable doubt; (v) the conviction and sentence awarded to accused 1 were bad in Law; (vi) the appellants have been falsely implicated by the prosecution; (vii) the circumstances relied upon by the High court are not sufficient to sustain the judgment of the High. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The retracted judicial confessions of accused I and 6 cannot be relied on against accused 6 in view of the fact that they were tried along alongwith accused 5 and 7 only. [799B] 2.1 The retracted Judicial confessions of the two accused are admissible under section 32 of the Evidence Act and the confirmation of the conviction is not required in this case. [781C D] 2(a) The retractedjudicial confession of a person accused of an offence under section 27 of the Indian Evidence Act can be used against him only if it is corroborated by other evidence. [783F G] (b) The High court has considered the evidence and dismissed the appeal filed by the State for enhancement of sentence. [784G] 2.(a) It is well settled that the Supreme Court does not interfere with the judgment or order of acquittal passed by the trial court unless it is shown to be perverse or based on no evidence or there are glaring infirmities in the reasoning of the trial Judge. [779D E] (c) The conviction and sentences awarded to the appellants under section 364 read with s.120B I P. C. are set aside. [780E F] (d) The appellants are acquitted of the charge under section 201 read with S.120 B I. It is not necessary for them to show that they have been convicted of any offence under S.302 read with 34 I P C or S.201 I. The conviction of the appellant under section 307 read with Ss. 120B, I.PC. and S.34 I. PC. is set aside and the appellants are convicted of the offence under s.302 I.Ps. and the sentence awarded by the Trial Court under section 392 read withs.120A I.I.P., is maintained.

The appellant executed a will in favour of his father, the respondent. The testator died on August 22, 1945 and his son was brought up by his widow, the appellant. On August 22 the appellant filed a suit for partition of the properties between himself and his wife. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the will was not proved to be the last will and testament of the testator and that it was her will in the sense that it represented her intentions. Held, that the evidence of the appellant himself was considered by the learned judge and his conclusion was based on a consideration of the evidence led by him. The High Court had rightly held that there was no evidence to prove the execution of the will. The evidence of this witness was corroborated by the appellant 's case about the execution and the dispositions in the will and the evidence adduced by the respondent on the question of attestation of the Will was highly improbable. The onus was upon him to establish that the testator had really understood its contents, and he had put his signature on it when she was in a sound and disposing state of mind. The burden was on him to prove that the execution was signed by him and that he understood the nature and effect of the dispositions before she put her signature to the document. The appellant had not discharged this onus by proving that the testatrix had really understanding its contents. The presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Act is a rebuttable one and it would be sufficient if the Court accepts the evidence as true, but where the evidence is clear and unambiguous, the court has to accept the same and act upon it. In the present case no doubt the appellant had signed the will in his own free will but he did not at all support the appellant"s case regarding previous instructions because according to him the testatrix was in sound and disposed state of her mind and that she understood the terms of the disposition before she made the will, and that the recitals in the document were highly improbable; and the High court had rightly found that it had been proved beyond reasonable doubt.

The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of Arc Carbons, known as "Cinema Arcocors" and also a "component parts of motor vehicles". The goods were sold by it to various persons. The sales tax authorities levied sales tax on these sales under section 3(1) (a) of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957. The appellant challenged the levy before the High Court. The High Court held that the main use of the are carbons was not "electrical goods" falling within entry 41 of Schedule 1 of the Act and that they fell under Entry 41 of the second schedule to the Act. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant company that (i) the words "electricity goods" in item 41 of Sch. 1 of Andhra Pradesh State General Sales tax Act, could not be said to have been used for goods sold for agricultural purposes merely because some of them are also sold to agriculturists for agricultural purpose; and (ii) the use of these words was not a "electric goods", falling within Entry 41, of Schedule I of the Madras General Sales Taxation Act, 1958. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The term "electronic goods" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. It will be noticed that the entry does not relate to goods sold or to agricultural purposes only but also to goods produced for agricultural pur poses. [562 E] 2. The word "electony" is employed in the Schedule to describe articles which may be manufactured for a particular kind of instrument of gadget only, the article manufactured to serve as a part of a particular type of apparatus would not cease to be covered by the intended entry merely because a purchaser makes some other use of it. [563 E] 3. The expression "electuring electrodes" is defined in the Act to mean "to perform any function or act which is necessary for the purpose of performing such functions". It will include all goods which are ordinarily used as part of the equipment, and which are required for use in projectors or other cinematographic equipment. [564 G] 4. The words "parts thereof" are used in several entries, such as entry 41, List I, even where an entry relates to parts manufactured for using a particular types of instrument. It would be noticed from the fact that they are known as 'electrical articles ' in the market. This is evident from the word "accessories" which is used therein in various entries, namely, Entry 41. [565 G] 5. The definition of "electures" is given in the explanation to section 2(g) of Act. It does not include electric power. [567 A B] 6. The use of words "for use" in Item 41, list 1, is used for the carbon, which may having been manufactured, for use for a specified kind of instruments of gAD, would not be covered under Entry 18 of the Second Schedule to the Andhra Act. [568 G H] 7. The fact that the are known and are known in the trade as "cinema" is not a relevant factor to attract the tax under entry 18 of Second Schedule. [569 B C] 8. The meaning of this entry can only be satisfactorily determined in the light of the language of the entry itself considered in the context in which it occurs. [570 G H; 571 A] 9. The Act does not deal with the carboxy and they are used for search lights, signalling, stage lighting, or where powerful lighting for photography or other purposes may be required, could never detract from the classification to which the carbon iss belong. [571 C D] 10.

The petitioners are the owners of a quarry lease or any other mineral concession granted under the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966. The petitioners were granted mining leases in respect of minor minerals by the State Government for the period from 1 7 1985 to 30 10 1985. The State Government issued an order on June 26, 1985 in exercise of its powers conferred by section 15 of the Act amending the Gujarat Minerals (Regulation and Development) Rules, 1966 with effect from 1st July, 1985 substituting the original rule 21 of the Rules by a new rule 21. The respondents challenged the validity of the said notification in a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the royalty levied and covered under the Rules should be applied only for mineral development and since the said royalty is being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State, the levy was bad; and that the impugned notification in question was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The Act is passed for devel opment of minerals from one State to another for the activity of quarrying does not involve any movement as such. [408B] 2.1 The Act has been passed for public interest and purposes by making a classification for purposes of implementing the policy of the Central Government. The statute and the Rules are in the nature of subordi nate legislation. They are intended to be used for the purpose of implementing a policy of granting leases, mining leases or other mineral concessions in re spect of minor mineral. [416C D] 2:2 In the instant case, the petitioners have not made any attempt to establish that there is any movement in the public interest. The only thing required is to see whether there is a reasonable nexus between the classification for purpose of the proviso to rule 21 to show concession in the matter of payment of royalty and the social policy underlying the Constitution, the statute and Rules. [414D E] 2 :3 The fact that section 15 does no authorise the State Govern ment to show such concession while promulgating the Rules which are in nature of subordinate legislation is also of no consequence. No express power need to conferred on such subordinate authority in order to make a classification in any way the freedom guaranteed under Article 301 of the Constitu tion regarding movement of goods from one state to another.

The appellant was the founder of a temple. He took a different view and proceeded on the basis that trusteeship of the temple was not hereditary. The High Court held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Madras Act 19 of 1951. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The office of a hereditary Trustee is in the nature of property. It is an office which is capable of being managed by a person who has no right to manage it. [445 B] (2) The expression "regulated by usage" in section 6 (9) means not hereditary but must be construed as including all persons who may have been appointed to a post in the temple. [427 C D] (3) The word "control" is used in the sense of administration of religious institutions. It includes all matters which are usually associated with religious practices and ceremonies. [416 E F] (4) The words "regulated" and "succession to this office" in the section mean that on the death of an existing mahant, his chela does not succeed to the office as a matter of course because the successor acquires a right only by appointment and the authority to appoint is vested in the assembly of the bairagis. [414 D E] (5) The appellant was appointed as a hereditary trustees under section 6 of the Act. He did not hold any such post for a period of one year. He was elected to that office. [413 F G] (6) The appointment of the appellant as a trustee in the present case is for a fixed period of One year and not for life. It was therefore difficult to hold that the office of the appel lant was hereditary within the definition of section 2(9). [414 C D].

The appellant was charged under section 302 IPC and sentenced to death. The prosecution case was that the deceased was sleeping on a bench outside his house in the open space where he was sleeping and when he went near his brother who was sleeping, he saw the accused running away from the place of occurrence. He was also seen by PW 4 with the appellant. The trial court acquitted the second accused but convicted him under section 201 IPC and sentencing him to death and sentenced him to life imprisonment. On appeal the High Court acquitted the third accused. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the testimony of PW 4 in the first information report is not a very serious infirmity since the witness may not have seen the other; (ii) the evidence of PW4 in the second information report stands contradicted by the medical evidence and (iii) the High court has not considered the intrinsic quality of the evidence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was not right in convicting the appellant on the sole testimony of a single witness. [710E] 2. The evidence of the sole witness is corroborated by the contents of the FIR. The very fact that this witness could be persuaded to substitute PWs 1, 2 and 3 for his deceased brother as chasing the assailants, degrades him from the status of an absolutely reliable witness. It is not possible to accept that he would not mention about this fact in the First Information Report. [ 709B] 3. The testimony of the second eye witness cannot be considered as a very weak infirmity since it has been rejected with reference to the first accused who was on the same boat with the deceased. [610E F] 4. The mere fact that the witness has stated in the earlier report that the appellant saw PW 1 running away after the assault is true, it is difficult to appreciate how he would be able to appreciate that he could not mention the fact in his first information Report. If the statement of PW 3 is to be believed, the crowd had gathered at the place where he fell dead and the deceased fell down after the attack was true, there is no reason why he would have seen that the persons who might have already escaped. [700F G] 5. The fact that PW 4 had stated in his First Information report that he saw PW1 running away while running away would not ask PW 4 to inform PW 4 who arrived at the spot a little later, for information with regard to the assailants. There is no evidence on record to show that PW4 was present at the time of occurrence when he came running. [ 700H; 700A] 6. The first information statement is true that the accused had stated that he had seen PW 1 going away from his house and running away. But the fact that he has stated that the dead body was found at No. 1 does not make any difference because the evidence in the case stands contradicted both by the testimony in court on a very material point. [1, H] 7. The statement of the first witness is not corroborated by his contents. It may be true that those who gathered would not asking PW 4, who arrived near his deceased elder brother about the accused ran away from there. But it is not difficult to say that he did not see the assailants who might had already escaped and that the evidence was not a mere chance witness. The other witnesses are not independent witnesses. They have been declared hostile by the prosecution. [750B C] 8. The second eye witnesses were not examined in court for the purpose of corroborating PW 4. If their version is to he believed, they would be wholly reliable.

The respondent, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax in the hands of the Income tax Officer under section 34(1)(b) read with section 24B of the Indian Income tax Act. The respondent claimed that the amounts received by him as heirs and legal representatives of Amarchand after his death should be deemed by the fiction incorporated in sub section (1) to be income received by the deceased person before his death and that the amount was liable to be assessed under section 24 B(1). The Income tax officer rejected the claim. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the payments were not taxable as they were made by the heirs and Legal representatives of the deceased Amarchand and were therefore not liable to pay out of the estate of the respondent. The Tribunal however held that these amounts were not liable for income tax under section 4(1) (b) of the Act, but only those which were received by a person who was alive. On reference, the High Court held that on a correct interpretation of section 24A the amounts which were sought to be taxed and which had been held not to be liable to tax were not exempt from income tax. The Commissioner of Income tax appealed to this Court. Held: (i) The words "or any tax which would have been payable under this Act if he had not died" in sub s.(1) of section 4 of the , are wide enough to include all persons who were alive and who could be assessed as income tax on the death of a person before the death. The expression "or other legal representatives" in section 24(B) means that the heirs or legal representatives are liable to make good any part of the income received in the previous year. (ii)The words "any person" in s.24A mean that irrespective of the date of receipt of income receivable by a deceased person, if the income is received by his heirs and other legal representative after his life time, they are liable for payment of tax just as the deceased would have be assessed to tax under the Act. (iii)The expression "any other legal heir" in the section means that irrespective Of the date when the income was received or the death had not taken place. The words 'or any liability which arose ' in sub sections (1), 2 and 3 of s 24B are wide and include all those who were liable to payment of income tax out of their estate. The word "person" is used in a wider sense than that of an ordinary person. In the present case, the amounts were sought by the respondent as heirs of Amar Chand after his wife died and therefore they were not assessed as Income tax under s.4(1), (b).

The petitioner, a member of the Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959, were promulgated by the State Government under section 3 of the Act. The petitioner challenged the validity of these rules on the ground that they contravened article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it was not made in exercise of the power conferred by the proviso to article 309(2) of the Constitu tion. Held: (i) The word "public employment" in section 3 is used in a wide sense and includes all persons employed in any department or office under the Government of, or any local or other authority within the territory of India or Union territory. The expression "public service" in the proviso means public services and includes services which are either expressly or by necessary implication excluded from the purview of the definition. (ii)The word "Public Employment" is used to denote a group of persons who have been appointed directly by promotion or by transfer to posts reserved under the State Public Service Commission for their own benefit, and not as a matter of right. The word 'public employment ' in section 2(g) of that Act includes all non gazetted Government servants. (iii)The expression "Public employment" is not defined in the Act but has been used in the sense of employment in a department or an office under a State Government. The definition of public employment in section 4 of the , does not include employment in any other department or authority within its territory. (iv)The words "public services" in sub section (1) of section 3 are wide enough to cover all non residential persons who are employed in the State or Union Territory as a condition of employment. The words "under the Government ' to which the word is used are not defined and therefore, they cannot be construed as meaning public service.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr Post Office. He was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Offices Act, 1898 and in two of them he was convicted under section 53 of the Act and in one of them was sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months. The High Court accepted the evidence of the prosecution witnesses and acquitted him of all the charges. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the appellant had secreted the letter just because it was found in an almirah which is said to have been in his exclusive possession, and (2) the mere fact that he was in the exclusive possession of the house and the almirah did not amount to any theft. HELD : (i) The prosecution has failed to prove that these letters were in the joint possession of appellant 's father and of which the key was furnished by the father. [414 D] (ii)The mere fact of seizure of the articles does not make it a case of theft. It is sufficient if the point to be established is whether the almirah was in his possession exclusively or even jointly with his father. If that is so, the taking away of the article by the appellant from the post office (if that is how he came by the articles) would be theft but it has not been found that he committed any theft and therefore the taking of the ornaments by the key is an offence under section 54 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

The appellant was the Secretary of a Panchayat Samiti. The Sarpanch of the Panchayat, who had been appointed as the Chairman of the Samiti, was not present at the time when the meeting was held. He was also not prepared to go to Tehsil but was presenting before the Panchayat whatever he had got in his possession. The appellant filed an application under article 227 of the Constitution challenging the order of the Sub Divisional Magistrate staying further proceedings before him. The High Court admitted the application and stayed further proceedings. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High court did not appreciate that the so called affidavit which was filed before the Panchas was in fact not an affidavit properly sworn to or a certified copy of the order He had no opportunity to explain his conduct. [117 D] (ii) The appellant 's application for stay was not accompanied by an affidavit duly sworn to and signed by him. It was not made after the proceedings on that date had commenced. [118 E] (iii) The order sheet did not show that any application was made before the Nyaya Panchayat. No application was filed in the Court of the Nyaya panchayat, nor was there any thing in the order sheet to show that the appellant 'rejected the objections raised by the Sarpanch and inadequacy of the evidence contained therein regarding the stay order alleged to have been passed by the High Court. [119 G] (iv) The record shows that the Sarpanch had not filed an affidavit before the High Commissioner, nor did he file any affidavit in support of his allegations. It is true that in certain cases proceedings can be adjourned to enable the parties to file better proof, but a judicial officer is not bound to do so and if he bona fide does not in his discretion adjourn proceedings, it cannot be said that he has committed contempt of court.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302, I.P.C., for causing the death of Sheo Sahai and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court dismissed his appeal against conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the entire report dictated by the appellant at the Police Station was inadmissible in evidence as its contents were not supported by any medical evidence, and that the extra judicial confession together with the circumstances relied on by the High Court had been wrongly rejected by the trial court. HELD : (i) The High Courts erred in rejecting the statement of the appellant about the appellant 's confessing to him that he had murdered Sheo Sahai. [211 G] (ii) The evidence of the approver was corroborated by Paley Singh, P.W. 2 who stated that the appellant had a bath in the Canal at night in the canal and had said that he did not see the appellant in the field on account of the crops being not very high. The fact that he was the sword which was stained with human blood at the time of murder is sufficient to establish conclusively that the person who possessed it so shortly after the murder of a person with whom he had enmity, had committed the murder. [212 B C] (iii) The extra judicial confessions of the accused to the police officer were not admissible in evidence under section 32 of the Evidence Act as there was good independent evidence with respect to the four matters mentioned in the report and relied on. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the electoral roll of the State Legislative Assembly on the ground that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rolls and Selection of Councillors) Rules, 1963. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the whole election process was vitiated on the basis of the defective electoral roll. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court had committed an error in not following the procedure prescribed for the purpose. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court has rightly dismissed the writ petition. [495C] 1.2 The High Courts have failed to follow the procedure laid down by law and have acted in a manner which is contrary to the well settled principles of natural justice. [498E] 1:3. The failure to comply with Rule 4 (1) and (2) of Rules 4(2) is fatal to the election petition. It is not the case of the petitioners that they did not know immediately after the publication of the notice under Rule4(1). They did not even know immediately thereafter when the notice was issued. [500F] 1 :4. The procedure prescribed by law for the preparation and presentation of electoral rolls is a mandatory one. It cannot be said that the failure to do so in the instant case amounts to an error on the face of record. [501A B] 1I:5. The appellants were entitled to the issue of the writ prayed for as of right and the High Courts had committed no error in dismissing the petition. The writ petition was rightly dismissed by the High. [50C D] 1,6. The election process has been completed on December 31, 1978 and the poll is held on December 30, 1978. It was notified that the nominations could be filed on and after November 25, 1978 but the poll was not possible. No satisfactory explanation was given in the course of the petition by the petitioners as to why they delayed the filing of the election till December 28, 1978 even though they knew that there was an error.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1947. In 1949, it entered into a contract with the respondent company for the supply of electricity to its factory at Ahmedabad. The agreement provided that the Company would pay to the company Rs. 1,00,000/ per annum on or before 30 10 1967 and the balance sheet and profit and loss account would be submitted within one month from the date of commencement of the contract. In 1966, the respondent filed a complaint against the appellant under section 134 of the 1913 Act alleging that the appellant had failed to comply with the requirements of section 220 of the 1956 Act. The trial court held that the respondent was guilty of the offence under section 135 of the Act and sentenced him to imprisonment for one month and also to pay a fine of Rs. 2,000. On appeal by the company, the High Court set aside the order of conviction and sentence and directed the appellant to pay to it Rs. 3,000 as compensation. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The failure to comply within the period prescribed under section 220(2) of the , or section 220 Of the Act, or section 221 of the Companies Act, 1913, did not make him liable under the provisions of section 134. [419 F] (2) Section 134 lays down that after balance sheet is laid before a general body, there can be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirement of the Sub section (2). The provision in section 134 lays out that if the balance sheets are not adopted at the general meeting before which it is laid, a statement of that fact and of the reasons therefore have to be annexed to the balance Sheet and to the copies thereof required to be filed with the Registrar. If no balance sheet was laid before the general body then there could be no doubt that no copy of the balancesheet so laid should be sent to the Registrar for being prepared. [420 G H] (3) The provision under section 132 of the Indian Companies Act and section 220 are mandatory in character and do not make it obligatory on the Directors to file the list of books and profit or loss account before an annual general meeting is a condition precedent to the requirement that copies of such documents so laid before, a general meeting should be filed before the Registrar.[420 A B] (4) The provisions of sections 134 and 220 are directory in character. [411 C D] (5) The punishment under these sections is for default in filing copies of the books and profits and loss accounts before an Annual General Meeting is made obligatory. But section 134 provides that after a balance sheet has been laid before any general body and for not sending a statement or to comply therewith, it may expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of the Acts. [414 D E] (6) The penalty under these Sections is for failure to file copies of balance sheets or profit and Loss account before the company in the general meetings. If the requirements are complied with even then the persons concerned would be liable for punishment for that default. [416 F G] (7) Section 132 lays down a condition that after the balance book has been prepared, a copy of such balance sheet shall be filed along with the register and a failure to do so is made punishable under sub section (4). The proviso to this sub section provides that if any person fails to comply, within the time prescribed, the Registrar may impose a penalty for default. Under section 132(2), the failure to furnish a copy or to furnish such statement of the fact that the balance Sheets were not adopted, would be punishable under section 221. [413 F G; 414 A B]. (8) The proviso is in two parts. The first part provides that where any person has failed to file a list of the accounts and profit & loss account within the prescribed time or sub section(1) of section 132, he shall be liable to punishment for such default.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the object of the impugned Act is to show that it is based on a reasonable classification of persons to whom or the offences in respect of which the procedure laid down in it is to apply and hence it is necessary to ascertain whether it is actually based on such a classification. The object of section 5 (1) is to provide for speedier trial of certain offences and not to punish any particular case or classes of cases or classes thereof, or class of cases as the State Government may by general or special order in writing direct. The Act does not contemplate a single trial of several offences but only one trial of all such offences. It is the State which has to make an application under section 6 (1), and it is the state government which can make the necessary classification for the purpose of making the provisions applicable to the procedure prescribed by it. The scheme of the Act shows that it was intended to provide a speediers trial of some offences, but not all offences or classes or cases as a whole. It does not by its own force make the special procedure provided in the Act applicable to all persons and to all offences, except those mentioned in section 5. The provisions of the statute are designed to achieve the object which is intended to be achieved by the Act. The classification of offences or the cases, for, in the absence of any special circumstances, cannot be regarded as a reasonable basis for classification.

The appellant was a Radiologist in the Medical College of Delhi. He was appointed as an Associate Professor of Radiotherapy (ex officio) both by the University of Delhi as well as by the Maulana Azad Medical College. The post of Associate Professor was advertised by the Central Health Service, Ministry of Health and Family Planning, Department of Health, New Delhi, inviting applications for the post of Assistant Professors in the said college. The appellant was selected by the Selection Committee constituted under Rule 8(2) of the Central Civil Services (Classification, Control & Appeal) Rules, 1965. He filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the selection and appointment of the appellant as Associate Professor. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the teaching experience gained by the appellant was not sufficient to entitle him to be appointed to the post. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the post in question is a clinical post while that of Associate Professors of Radiology is a teaching post; (ii) the qualifications and experience prescribed for appointment to the said post are different and the appellant who had been substantively appointed to that post cannot be appointed by direct recruitment as Professor of radiotherapy or Associate Professor in the Willingdon Hospital or the Safdarjang Hospital and (iii) the status of Associate professor of Radiologist cum Associate Professor is akin to that of honorary Professor or Associate Professors in Willing don Hospital or Safdarjung Hospital and the mere designation of the said appellant as such does not give him a right to hold the post, because he did not possess at least five years ' teaching experience as Reader/Assistant Professor in Radiology (exclusive) in the willing don hospital or the Shahdara. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The post in dispute is a medical college and it is a post belonging to specialists Grade II. It is a research post. It has been designated as such by the Indian Medical Council of India. [802C] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellant had been continuously holding the post for more than 17 years. He had been regularly appointed to this post and he was also confirmed in that post with effect from October 9, 1964. The appointment letter clearly stated that the appellant would be eligible for appointment as Associate professor in the Mahammed Azad Medical college. [883D] 1:3. In view of the fact that the Central Government has been using his services as such for teaching the post graduate and under graduate students of the Manaecology (Ex officio) in a teaching hospital like the appellant, it is not possible to say that the post was a clinical one. [894E] 1 :4.

The appellant company was a registered trade union of workmen employed in the respondent 's region. The workmen were paid wages at the rate of Rs. 95 per day. In the year 1962, the Company made an application to the Industrial Tribunal for fixation of minimum wage of the workmen and for payment of bonus on that basis. The Tribunal fixed the minimum wage at Rs. 90 per day and in respect of the same, it took into account the total number of workmen who had to be paid production bonus. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The Tribunal was right in holding that there were other industries in the region which could be compared with the appellant 's industry in the area. [682 D] (ii) The minimum wage payable by those industries is very small and almost insignificant as compared with those in the Company 's area. In this case, however, there was nothing to show that the company was providing any amenities which were different from the amenities that are being provided by those concerns in the regions which are being used for the purpose of fixing minimum wage. [641 D] The Tribunal had rightly held that the minimum wages payable by the industries were very small. [651 E] (iii) The workmen are not providing any such amenities as are different from those that are required by those concern in the Region which are to be used for maintenance of the industry. They are not entitled to any additional benefits under the Act. [661 F] (iv) The award was made on the basis of the evidence adduced before it and there was no reason why the Tribunal should have proceeded to fix the minimum rate of wages in the company on the ground that it was based on the circumstances that, according to the workmen, the bonus in their case was being calculated as equivalent to three months ' basic wages. [671 F G] (v) The finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal that there was a substantial industry in this region comparable with the Company in the other region is not correct.

The assessee, a partnership firm, was carrying on business as commission agents. The Income tax Officer issued to the assessee a notice under section 148 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961, for the assessment year 19 19 ' and called upon him to furnish within 30 days from the date of service of the notice a return showing all or any of the requirements which may be included in a notice. The assessee filed an application under section 147 of the Act before the Income tax officer for issue of a notice on the ground that he had failed to comply with the requirements of section 148 and section 151(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Commissioner rejected the application holding that the impugned notice was invalid inasmuch as it did not comply with section 151 (2) Of the Act. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The notice under s 148 is valid only if it does not comply within 30 day of service. If the assessee fails to do so, the Income. tax Officer has no jurisdiction to issue a notice in respect of that period. In the present case, the assessee did not have the opportunity to make a return under section 139(2). The notice was issued on June 3, 1966 and it was served on the assessee on July 1, 1966. The notice dated June 3. 1966 was valid only for the purpose of issuing a notice of demand under section 151.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was carrying on business in the name and style of 'M/s. Doypack Ltd., and its partners. The firm consisted of three partners, namely, (1) M/s Doyppack Ltd.; (2) M.L.A. and (3) M, L.A., and the appellant was a partner in a firm. The Income tax Officer held that the business must have been charged to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918, but he did not accept the contention of the appellant that the firm was liable to pay income tax on the profits and gains of the period between the end of the previous year and the date of such succession. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that as a result of the splitting up there was a discontinuance of the original business at the date when the partition took place, the family became entitled to relief under section 25(3) Of the Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1939, and that the income, profits and losses of the firm were liable to be taxed under the Act of 1918. The Appellate Tribunal held that there was discontinuance of a business at that time and on such discontinuance the family ceased to exist and its business was carried on thereafter by two independent firms, for the document of October 30, 1943 had referred to the annexures C 1 and C 11 as constituting two independent partnerships and proceeded to revoke them both. The High Court in reference held that though the partners constituted a separate firm, they were not liable to tax for the period prior to the partition and on that footing the family was liable for the income tax. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The mere fact that the partner was not taken on in the original partnership did not make him liable to income tax for that year. [107 B] (ii) The question whether a firm is entitled to the benefits of section 25 (4) of the Income Tax Act, 1922, or whether it is liable to payment of tax under section 26(3), as was the case here, was one which arose out of the partition in 1948 and not in 1947. [108 E] (iii) The fact that he was not taking on in a original business also shows that the original firm was not in existence at the time when the partitioned took place. [109 G H] (iv) The High Courts were right in holding that the Tribunal was right in treating the firm as a separate and distinct partnership. [110 C D] (v) The Tribunal was wrong in treating it as a new partnership. It is not correct to say that the partners constituting the appellant at the moment of the transfer in 1948, formed a separate partnership. They were merely members of a joint family and were not entitled to any share therein. [111 E F] (vi) The word "partner" in section 25 means a person who has been allotted a business under the provisions of the Act. It does not mean a person whose name is entered in the register of partners.

The appellant, a Hindu Mitakshara coparcener, was born in the year 1947. He had two sons, namely, his two sons and the widow of his two daughters. The first son died in 1954. The second son died on September 1, 1956. The third son died before the coming into force of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, and the appellant 's mother was the only surviving son. The appellant filed a suit for partition of the coparcenary property claiming that there was no prior partition and that the plaintiff was entitled to a share in the joint family properties. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the suit properties belonged to the joint Hindu Mitakshara coparcenary and that there were six sharers in the coparcenary properties, that there had been no prior division and that it was not possible for the appellant to get a share therein. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the property belonged to a joint family and that, therefore, there was a prior partition. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the suit property belonged exclusively to the Joint Hindu Mitakshara Family and that in any event, the appellant was entitled only to a half share; (ii) the respondent 's share must be ascertained by adding the share to which she is entitled at a notional partition during her husband 's life time and the share which she would get in her husband"s estate upon his death. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The property belonged not only to the coparcenary but also to the widow. [724B] 2.1 A joint Hindu coparcenary is a creature of statute and it cannot be created by any statute. It is not open to the court to create a new coparcenary in respect of the joint property which has been partitioned during her life time between himself and his two wives. [764C D] 2(a) The rule that a coparcener can obtain a share only when he is entitled to claim partition or where there are several coparceners in the family, is not seriously disputed. [774D E] 3.1 In order to ascertain the share of heirs in the property of a deceased coparcener it is necessary in the very nature of things, and as the very first step, to ascertain whether a partition had actually taken place between the plaintiff 's husband and his sons, two must be determined according to the terms of the testamentary instrument, if any, made by the deceased and since there is none in the instant case, by the application of the rules of intestate succession contained in sections 8, 9 and 10 of the Act. [754E F] 3(b) The inevitable corollary of this position is that the heir will get his or her share in a joint Hindu family property upon his birth. [765F G] 4.1 The inevitable consequence of the rule is that if a partition has actually taken effect during her lifetime, it must be presumed to have taken place immediately before her death. If the law provides otherwise, the rule of intestate inheritance contained in section 6 does not apply. [664G H] 4(a). In an important aspect, the case before us is stronger in the matter of working out the fiction because in a partition of coparcenary property, the interest of a Hindu coparcener "shall be deemed to be the share in that property that would have been allotted to him if a disruption of that property had taken place before his death". [723B C] 4.(b) In order that a son may obtain a 1/4th share and two, that the share should be determined by adding 1/3rd share which he would get on his death, it is sufficient to show that the deceased had not been in possession of any share in his coparcenary property because after all the three daughters had become co owners.

The respondent was appointed as a Class II employee in the appellant Corporation on or after 1st September, 1956. He was later promoted to the post of Assistant Manager (General) on or before 31st October, 1956 and was confirmed with effect from 1st November, 1956 by an order dated 30th April, 1957. The respondent challenged the said order by a writ petition in the High Court which allowed the same holding that the employees of Class I or Class II appointed to the service of the Corporation on and after 1 st September,1956 were not entitled to continue in service beyond 60 years of age. The appellant Corporation filed an appeal before this Court against the judgment of the High court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The respondent was not entitled for the benefit of regulation 19(2) as he had been promoted to a Class I post or class II post. [223E] (2) The regulations framed by the Corporation under section 49(2)(b) were in terms applicable to the transferred employees who became the employees after 1th September, 1957 and therefore, they could not be said to have been made applicable to them. [225F G] (3) The order of transfer was passed on or about 31st March, 1956, and the respondent was given three months ' notice or salary in lieu thereof. The order was issued on or around 1st April, 1956 after the date of retirement of the respondent. [226A B] (4) The Corporation could not have made any provision for giving effect to the said regulation 19 by extending it at its discretion to the employees who had joined service prior to 1st Sept., 1956. [227C D] (5) The High Court erred in striking down Regulation 19(1)(b). [228D] (6) The scheme of the Act was not applicable to a transferred employee who became an employee of the corporation under section 11 of the and therefore he could not claim any benefit thereunder.

The appellants, who were the Judges of the High Court, filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the order of the Full Bench of the Punjab and Haryana High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the allegations made against them were not proved. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the letter was addressed by the deponent to the President of India, with copies to others with the sole object of conveying the opinion that the public expression by the Hon 'ble Judge of his personal views on controversial political matters con cerned the merits and demerits of the present system of Government was not in keeping with the well accepted role of a Judge. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The letter dated 20 February 1975 addressed by one of the members of the Bar Association, Bhiwani to the Chief Justice of Punjab and State High Court was addressed to the Governor of Haryana. The appellants were not aware of any such contempt. They had no occasion to complain that the Judges who wrote the letter in question were not present at the meeting of the Judge of the said High Court or to lower the authority or undermine the prestige of the learned Judge or of the Hon"ble Court or the Chief justice of Punjab & Haryana High Courts. [243E G] 2. The contempt proceedings are dropped. [244B C] 3. The matter did not constitute any contempt. The respondents were not guilty of any contempt of court. They were not entitled to any relief in the present case. [245C] 4. The apology was tendered by the appellant and others who had been given an opportunity to explain their conduct. The appellant had no cause for the same. He had no right to complain against the Judges. [246D] 5. The question whether the appellants committed contempt of Court is a matter which should be determined on facts whether the Judge concerned did speak on the matters ascribed to him before the court would take any action against the persons who would criticise the Judge 's speech. [247E] 6. The word " contempt" in section 2(c) of the Act means any act or omission which is done by a person in pursuance of his duty as a judge or in any manner to lower his authority or to cause injury or annoyance to any other person. It does not mean that the contempt must be committed by a Judge or a court in discharge of office of a judge. [248F] 7. The expression "any act or proceeding" used in section 3(c), means any proceeding or proceeding which is pending on the date of the publication of the notice under section 4. It is not a case where the speech of any Judge is criticised and if it becomes a disputed question of fact as to whether any Judge did speak or not as is alleged by the writer the matter would have to be ascertained by the court on facts, whether the judge concerned did speaks on the matter before the Court would take some action against those who would criticism of the administration of justice. [249G H] 8. The words "any person" in sub section (1) of section 2 of the Prevention of Corruption Act are wide enough to include a Judge who is guilty of contempt of any court. The use of the word "person" in the sub section makes it clear that there is to be a finding of committal of contempt. [250A B] 9. The Court has to see whether the Judges concerned did so on the facts and circumstances of each case. If the speech is criticised, then the matter will have to he ascertained by court on the basis of facts whether or not the Judge did speaks or not. [251C D] 10. In the absence of such a finding no question arises for acceptance of apology. The matters did not constituted any contempt and were not liable to be dealt with by the Court on facts. [252E F] 11. The Supreme Court has power to punish for contempt of itself.

The petitioner, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1948 49 under the Indian Income tax Act. The petitioner challenged the validity of section 5(1) of the Act on the ground that it contravened article 14 of the Constitution and was therefore not saved by article 14 Of the Constitution. Held, that the provisions of section 6(5) of Act XXXV of 1947 were valid and did not contravene article 14. The procedure prescribed by the impugned Act in so far as it affected the petitioner was a reasonable restriction within the meaning of article 19 (1)(f) of India. The impugned Act was therefore void. The provisions of the impugned section were not discriminatory and could not be said to offend article 14, because, under the provisions Of section 5 (1) the procedure prescribed in the impugned sections was a good substitute for that prescribed by Indian Income Tax Act. Held further, that section 6 (5) was valid as it contravened articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of Part III of the constitution. The object of the section was to provide for the imposition of reasonable restrictions on the right to carry on business in India and to make provision for securing their equitable distribution and availability at fair prices. The Act did not violate article 14 because, it contravened the provisions contained in article 19(6) of that Article. The classification made by the Act was based upon a rational basis and was not arbitrary or irrational. The fact that under the Act the procedure to be followed for catching evaded income was a relevant consideration for determining whether the assessee had evaded payment of tax would not make any difference, because the procedure laid down in section 34 of the Indian Incometax Act is a reasonable one and does not offend article 19.

The Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry, New Delhi (Respondent No. 1) was a "commercial establishment" within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Delhi Shops & Establishments Act, 1954. The Federation was established by an agreement dated January 21, 1956 with its members. The terms of the agreement were to be determined in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder. The respondent No. I was a company registered under the Companies Act, 1913. It had its registered office at Delhi. The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act and having its registered address at New Delhi, was carrying on business in the premises in question. The Company was established for the purpose of promoting the trade of the Federation or any part thereof for such consideration as the Federation may think fit and in particular for shares, debentures, etc. The members of the appellant 's Association were also members of a registered society known as "Ambalal" which was registered under section 2 (1) of that Act. The Society was registered on January 21. 1956. The Registrar of Shops and Establishments, Delhi issued notices to the Federation calling upon it to show cause why its establishment should not be terminated for breach of conditions of service of its members and also for payment of compensation for loss or damage caused by such termination. The Association filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice on the ground that the activities of the respondent No 1 were not "business" within section 2 of the . The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the activity of the Association was in the nature of business or trade and that it was not an "establishment" within Section 2(1) (d) of Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The activities of respondent No I were not 'business ' within the definition of " commercial establishment". [356 F] (ii) The activity of respondent 1 was in nature of a business or trading and it was immaterial whether its activities bring its premises within the ambit of a "shop" or a " commercial Establishment". It is immaterial whether the activities bring the premises within that category or a 'commercial establishment '. [356 G] (iii) The definition of 'business" in section 2,(5), does not necessarily mean something by which a profit is made. It will bear repetition that the Federation also publishes periodicals, bulletins etc. and issues the same to member free of this Court in R. K. Of course, that profit is ploughed back for the purposes of the Federal Court inR. K . Of course that profit was plouGDhed back. [337 B C] (iv) The word "business ' does not mean anything by which an activity carried on by it amounts to a busi (1)[1971] 1 S.C.R.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family consisting of himself and his brothers. The income from the agricultural land was assessed to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The assessee claimed that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. The Income tax Officer held that it had been a regular assessment of the income and did so on the ground that it could not be said that the receipt of the asses see was agricultural income within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of the Act. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer. The High Court in reference held that from the language of the letter of July 7, 1837 it was manifest that the right which was conferred was a right to a share of one fourth in the net land revenue collections after deducting costs of Tahsil establishment. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The source of the allowance or pension is the arrangement arrived at in 1837 and therefore, it is not agricultural income as defined in section 2(1)(a) of Act. [702 D] (ii) The words "in a sense related to land" are used in the context of the definition of agricultural Income tax. They are not intended to convey any idea of the nature of the right or privilege. [700 E] (iii) The income appropriated by the appellant as remuneration is not received by him as rent or revenue of agricultural lands but rests in the covenant in the deed to receive remuneration for management of the trust. [602 G H] (iv) The High Courts were right in holding that from a reading of the letters of July, 18 37, it was clear that the appellant had no beneficial interest in the land and did nothing more than what he had received as rent.

The petitioners in C.A. No. 441 of 1981 were appointed as Supervisors Grade II in different ordnance factories between 1962 and 1966 a nd they were promoted as Chargeman II on the basis of selection list prepared in the manner provided therei n, but their promotion was not made on completion of two years ' service as Supervisor 'A ' by its order dated 16th April, 1979. The petitioners filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the said orders and the same were dismissed. In the appeals to this Court it was contended that since Rule 8 of the Rules contemplated th at appointments by promotion were to be made on the recommendation of a Selection Committee constituted in accordance with the provisions of the Madhya Pradesh Hi gh Court 's Service Rules, 1975, the non promotion of the appellants was discriminatory being in violation of Article 16. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court has rightly held that the judgment of this Court dated 2nd February, 1981 in Civ il Appeal No. 442 of 1981 is completely silent on the point and the appeal w as allowed only on the ground that some Supervisors having been promoted as chargeman II by its ord er dated 16.4.1979 had come into force and had also come into existence the circular dated 6th November, 1962 which had superseded the circular of 6th Nov ous, 1962 and had provided that in future promotions of all such individuals will be effected in accordance wit ness with the normal rules and not merely on the completion of 2 years ' servi ce as Supervisor. [408C D] 1.2 The High Courts have rightly held t hat the judgment dated 2 nd February,1981 in C .A. Nos. 441/81 and 442/81 was completely silent about the effect of the order dated 2.2.1981 in which it had superseded its earlier order dated 6 th November, 1963 and had given a gov ernment to the appellants that they would be entitled to be treated as Chargemen t II on completion o f two years service as Supervisors 'A. The HighCourt has rightly observed that the appellants of this appeal have in pur poses of the orders passed by the High Courts dated 2 2 1981 in Civil Appeal No 441/1981 and 14 1 2 1981, which were filed after the decision of 2nd Febru ary, 1981.

The Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation (K.S.R.T.C.) was constituted under the Karnataka Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 to carry out the purposes of the Act. The Regional Transport Authority and the High Court held that the State Transport Undertaking would have preference over all eligible applicants for permits from the State transport undertaking. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Karnataka Road Transport Corpora tion (K S.R.) would have priority over other applicants who had applied for permits under section 47(1 H) of the Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 1984 and that the said preference would be given to applications for permits in respect of such number of tourist vehicles as the Central Government may, by notification, specify in this behalf. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Karnataka State Transport Undertakings (Ks. R.T.) Corporation (M.S.) Rules, 1984 are not ultra vires the provisions of sections 47(i H) and 47(2). [1015B] 2. Section 47(I H) provides that in the case of a notified route or notified area, where under section 68 F(1) the permit has to be necessarily granted to the State Road transport undertaking, in all other cases, the claims of all eligible applicant must be considered on merits, applying the rules of preference wherever the claims are approximately equal. [1016C] 3.

The respondent was a dealer in business of selling goods. The appellant, who was the registered owner of the business, sold the goods to the respondent on October 5, 1956 and the sale proceeds were credited into the account of the respondent. The respondent filed a suit for arrears of sales tax due from him on the ground that he had purchased the goods from the State Government as a dealer under section 19(1) of the Madras General Sales Tax Act 1939 (Madras Act IX of 1939). The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court in second appeal confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that Rule 21 A is ultra vires of the rule making power of the State Govern ment under section19(1)(a) of Madras General sales Tax Act, 1939 (Mad. IX of 1940). HELD: The word 'assessment ' used in section 19 (2)(c) does not include the power of recovering tax assessed from a person other than the assessee. It follows therefore that Rule21 A is beyond the rule made by the State Legislature under section 9(1), and cannot be utilised to enlarge the scope of section 10 regarding recovery and payment of tax from some other person other persons other than a "dealer" under the Act. [665 B C] The word assessment ' has been defined in section 2(c) of that Act as including all proceedings taken under the Madras Sales Tax (3rd Amendment) Act, 1956. Therefore, Rule 21A is beyond its rule making powers of the state Government either under section 10 or section 19 of the Act and cannot he utilised to extend the scope thereof to any particular person other wise.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk in the State of Saurashtra. He was dismissed from service on February 2, 1955. The respondent filed an application under section 33(2) (a) of the Bombay Civil Services Act, 1946 for a declaration that he continued to be in Government service till the date of his dismissal and for a decree for Rs. 1,000/ . The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that there had been a breach of article 311(2). In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts erred in holding that there was a breach Of article 311 (2) of Constitution as according to him there was no duty to supply a copy of the report of the enquiry held against him. HELD: The High Court erred in ordering a decree under section 31(2)(a) for Rs, 1,006/ . [922 D] The State of Bombay vs The Province of Bombay, ; , referred to. (1) The provisions of article 310(2), which are mandatory and not directory, do not apply to the case of arrears of salary earned by a public servant for the period that he was actually in office. It is true that the word 'actionable wrong other than breach of contract ' in section 60 of the Act does not include something more than torts, but even so where a suit is brought by a Government servant for arrears of pay, the decree more properly falls under section 61(2); it is true, as held by this Court in State of Tripura vs The province of East Bengal, (1962) Supp. 1 S.C.R. 869, that the words 'action able wrong other like breach of contracts ' in article 311 must be construed in their widest sense and not in narrow or technical sense. [923 D E] (2)(i) The expression 'actionabilityable wrong ' is wide enough to include all kinds of acts which have a direct bearing on the question whether they are done in good faith or for a collateral purpose. It does not mean mere irregularity, but merely an act done by a person who has no legal right to do it. [948 E] In the present case, the respondent was not concerned with the second contention but only with the third contention. The High Courts had erred in treating the respondent as a 'live ' and that the liability for payment of arrears was not a liability arising out of a contract but was a liability in respect of an actionable wrong other then the State. [947 G] (ii) The decree of the High court decreeing payment of Rs. 2,000 to the respondent did not suffer from any infirmity.

The appellants were adjoining colliery owners at Kujama. The respondents claimed that the suit was not barred by limitation and they had failed to prove that the respondents had knowledge of the alleged encroachment only within three years thereof. The trial court held that the defendants had encroached upon their coal mines on the northern side and removed coal from the encroached portion of the encroached area. On appeal, the High Court confirmed this finding. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Courts were in error in holding that the onus of proof to establish knowledge on the part of the respondents beyond the prescribed time was on the appellant; that the courts below had wrongly held that they had not given any such notice as required by section 80 C.P.C. and that the appellants had failed in their attempt to prove the fact that the respondent had knowledge about the encroachment only in the year 1941, which was within three yea years of the date of the filing of the suit; that no plan had been annexed to the lease deed executed in favour of the successors in interest of the appellant and the respondents were estopped from challenging the correctness of the finding of fact arrived at by the courts. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding on the assumption that the initial burden of proof was on respondents. [475 D] (ii) The onus of proving knowledge on a party to show that he had knowledge, of the existence of the encroachment, only within 3 years thereof, is upon him. In the present case, the appellant did not deny the fact of knowledge of it only in 1941 and there was no acceptable evidence on their part to establish that they came to know of the removal of coal by the appellant or their possession of the coal removed beyond three years prior to the suit. [498 E] (iii) The burden of proving the fact is on the person who asserts the existence, of a material fact and not upon the party who asserts it. In other words, he has to prove his own case.

The appellant was a crosscutter. The respondent terminated the services of the appellant under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders. The appellant challenged the termination on the ground that it was mala fide and was not bona fide. The tribunal held that the action taken by the appellant was bona fide and therefore its action could not be upheld as a bona fide exercise of the power conferred. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to inquire into the causes that led to termination of service under r 18(b). The Tribunal has the right to inquire whether there was in fact misconduct or not and if it is satisfied that the act done by the employer was a colourable exercise of power or as a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice, it would have jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. [824 D] (ii) The appellant had failed to satisfy the tribunal when the matter came before it for adjudication that the exercise of its power was bona bonafide and was in public interest. The Tribunal was therefore right in holding that the order terminating the services was bona fides. [884 F G] (iii) The employer could defend the action under r, 18(1) by leading evidence before the tribunal to show that there was misconduct and therefore the action was bona bona fide or was a result Of victimisation or improper unfair labour practices. [894 D E] (iv) The question whether the action of the employer in terminating the service of an employee is bona fide must be determined on the facts of each case. In the present case, the tribunal had held that there were misconduct and it could not therefore inquire into those causes that might have led to the termination of the services under r 17(a). [895 F G; 896 A] (v) The tribunal was right in taking the view that the discharge of the respondent was bona. fide and did not justify before it.

The respondent plaintiff filed a suit against the appellant defendant for declaration that he was entitled to a declaration that it was entitled pursuant to the agreement dated December 1, 1960, to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether the respondent was a lessee or not is one of fact depending on the facts and circumstances of each case. [445 B] (ii) The High Court has recorded a finding that the agreement was of the nature of a lease and that the consent decree operated as res judicata. [427 C D] (iii) The trial Judge had rightly held that the respondent 's suit was barred by the principle of res judicata under section 92 of the Evidence Act, because the question was already concluded by the consent decrees in suit No. 149 of 1960. [416 G H] (iv) The finding of the High court is set aside and the matter remitted to the trial Court for fresh decision on the question whether it was open to the respondent to lead evidence to show that the transaction between the parties of the year 1954 was in the nature or a lease.
