[414 C D, E F] (v) The suit was not barred by res judicata because the High Courts have recorded findings on the nature and character of the agreement. [413 G H; 414 A] (vi) The respondent 'could lead any evidence to prove that the document dated December, 1960 created a lease or an other character. [411 C D].

The respondent was appointed as a pilot Officer in the Indian Air Force and was confirmed on 1st June, 1983. He was later promoted to the post of Assistant Engineer in the year 1972. The petitioner challenged his appointment by filing a Writ Petition before the High Court contending that he was enti tled to be reinstated in service irrespective of the fact whether the Governor had extended the period of his appointment beyond 30th August, 1985. The High Court allowed the Writ Petition and directed the effect that the respondent was entitled to salary upto the period he was entitled for remain in service till 30th of August,1985 and not beyond that date unless there was a further extension. The State filed an appeal before this Court contending inter alia that the interim order passed by the High court on 10.7.86 could not be sustained and the Writ Appeal was liable to be dismissed. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have while setting aside the order of termination by its order dated 24.3.1988 directed that the respond ent should be reinstated with full back wages. [243E] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent had not urged before the Court that the order was not in the nature of a contract and the subsequent orders extending his period of appointment till 30.8. 1985 were liable to he ignored and that he should be treated as a person regularly appointed in Government service entitled to continue till he completed the age of 58 years. His only case was that the ad hoc order dated 10. 785 could not have been passed by him on 29.3 .1988 because his term of office had come to an end on 30th September, 1985 and no further order of extension of service could be passed by any authority. [244E G] 1:3. The respondent was not satisfied with the order allowing the Writ Petitioner as stated above. He proceeded to file a Review Petition claiming to be re spondent for reinstatement in service. His case was not that he had been given an opportunity to show cause against the order allow ing him to continue in service beyond 30. August,85. The order dated 26.7 1988 passed by High Court on review and restoring the judgment dated 24th March, 1988 passed in Writ Petition No. 36 of 1987 were liable t o be ignored and set aside. [245E G; 246A] 1 :4. The interim order did not and could not amount to a direction that the respon dents were entitled to be paid salary upto 30th October, 1985 when there was no order of extending his service till he complete the age Of 58 years, nor did it affect the jurisdiction of the High Courts to dispose of the Writ petition on merits as it did on 24. 3.1988. [246B] 1 5. The writ petitioner had not filed any review petition claiming that he could be reinstated only in the event of his reinstatement. His claim was not barred by limitation. He did not do so. He, therefore, proceeded to maintain the Writ Application on merits.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to rigorous imprisonment for seven years. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the High Court erred in holding that the evidence of P. 1 to 3 was more probable than the version of the prosecution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Courts should not interfere with the order of acquittal merely because another view is also possible. [368E] (2) In a case where two views are possible, the accused is entitled to the benefit of doubt arising from the possibility of duality of views. [369F] (3) The evidence of the eye witnesses has been corroborated by the evidence given in Court of Sessions. It is obvious that he must have been upset by the persistent refusal of the brother and mother of the deceased to send her with him to his house. [370G] Khem Karan & Ors. vs State of U.P., ; , referred to. (4) The fact that the appellant was a woman of 69 years old, before the occurrence, makes a gesture as if she was stabbing the deceased and that the deceased cried out 'Amma. The Inspector of Police P. W. W, W.W. 1, who was then posted at the house of the accused, prepared by him, prepared the scene of offence which was later taken over by the Inspector of police. He also stated that he went ahead with the further investigation and found the accused lying on the ground in front of the house by means of a rope. The Sessions Judge thought that when there were two conflicting versions given by the prosecution and the defence, the benefit should be given to the accused. [367A B] Khem Chand & Ors vs State, ; , applied. (5) In the instant case, the evidence was corroborated by what was mentioned in exhibit P. 2, the statement of the appellant to the effect that he saw the accused who was sitting by the side of the body on the cot making a gestures as if he was stabbing her and that he had been stabbed by means which he cried. The evidence was not sufficient to entitle an accused person to the benefits of doubt. [366B C] Khem Raj & Ors., vs State Of U.

The appellant, a Judge of the Supreme Court, was appointed as an Assistant Sessions Judge in January, 1978. He was removed from his office by an order dated May 27, 1978 passed under section 6(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The appellant challenged the said order before the High Court on various grounds including that he had been removed from service without holding any inquiry or giving him a reasonable opportunity to defend himself and that the order was mala fide. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) Section 6(i)(c), specifically enjoins that no court shall take cognizance of an offence punishable under section 5 of the Act alleged to have been committed by a public servant i.e. the Judge of a High Court, except with the previous sanction of the Central Government; and (ii) that the provisions of sections 6(2) and 6(3) are not applicable to the case of a Judge who is removed from office by the President in accordance with clause (4) of Article 124 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The power to punish a Judge under section 3(i) of Prevention of corruption Act,1947 is a special law enacted by Parliament under Article 124(5), even for investigation and proof of any misbehaviour alleged against a superior Judge instead of the general law was clearly visualised when the alleged misbehaviour is connected with his office. [216C D] 1.2 The word "court" in section 6 (i)(a) has to be given some meaning which would place the burden on the prosecution, howsoever light, to make out a prima facie case for obtaining sanction of competent authority under Section 6 of the . [217D E] 1:3. The word 'court ' is not defined in the Code of Criminal Procedure but it has been used in the sense in which it is used in section 2(g) of that Act. It has been held by this Court in State of Bombay vs Purushottam Jog Naik, ; , that a Judge or Chief Justice of a District Court cannot be removed from the office by any other person except by his removal from office in accordance With clause (a) of article 124 and (b) a special procedure enacted by the Parliament under article 124(4) is clearly visualized when the purported misbehaviour is dealt with by the Chief Justice. [217E F] 1 :4. The provisions contained in clauses 4 and 5 of Article 125 read with Article 2(h) of Constitution are clear pointer in the direction that the Parliament has not as yet considered it expedient to enact any such law for the trial and punishment on the charge of corruption of a superior judge, except by their removal from his post in the manner prescribed. [218H; 218A] 1 5. The words 'any person ' in clause (e) have to be read as a part of the scheme under which the public servant is required to furnish particulars of his assets with reference to which the disproportion and his inability to satisfactorily account can be inferred. Any provision which cannot apply to the Chief justice of India, cannot obviously apply to Judges of the High Courts or the Supreme court. [220B] 1 6. The expression 'any other person ' has to he given some interpretation which would placed the burden upon the prosecution as a whole and not on the accused who is sought to be proceeded against.

The appellant was a Sunri by caste. He challenged the election of the respondent to the State Assembly on the ground that he belonged to an independent caste which had nothing to do with the Sunri caste. The Tribunal held that the appellant belonged to the "Scheduled Caste" and not to a member of any Scheduled Caste. On appeal, the High Court set aside the decision of the Tribunal and directed the election petition to be dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the respondent had been wrongly excluded from the ' Sunri ' group because he belonged only to a smaller caste group of Sahas; (ii) the High court erred in holding that the respondent belonged to a larger caste group and not a member thereof; and (iii) the Tribunal was wrong in holding the appellant to be a member belonging to the Scheduled Caste specified in item 40. HELD: (i)(a) The word 'Scheduled Castes ' has been used in the expression "excluding Saha" in the item. It is not necessary that the word 'BC ' should have been included in item No. 40. [390 C] (b) The Tribunal was right in holding on the basis of the evidence that the appel lant belonged to 'Scheduled Caste ' and not 'BC". [391 D] (c) The High Court erred in setting aside the order of the Election Tribunal. [391 E] (d) The respondent had not established that he belong to a particular caste group within the meaning of item 40, as he was a 'Scheduled Tribe '.

The appellant was the tenant of a monthly rent of Rs. 2,000 and the respondent landlord paid him the sum of Rs 29,500 to the appellant as advance payment. The appellant refused to accept the amount on the ground that he had not been given an opportunity to pay the balance due in respect of the furniture and the documents that were handed over to him by the appellant. The Magistrate held that the appellant was guilty of an offence under section 19(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. On appeal the Presidency Magistrate acquitted the appellant but convicted him under section 20(1)(a) of that Act. The High Court on a reference made to it by the Presidency Magis trate held that there was no relinquishment of tenancy and that the document did not create any relinquishment. Held, that the word "relinquishment" in section 18 (1) (a) meant only an assignment of the tenancy and not a relinquishment. The word "distin quently" used in section 17(2), therefore, must be read as referring to an assignment by the tenant or tenant of his rights as such. The words "conveyed" in the Transfer of Property Act would have been more appropriate if the transfer was meant by surrender by the lessee or tenant. The intention of the legislature was that the transferee should have the right to receive the rent and not the relinquishment. In the present case there was a relinquishment of the rights of the appellant and therefore the transaction was one for the recovery of arrears of rent.

The appellant, a contractor, was awarded a contract for the supply of certain specified items of iron and steel. The workmen were paid Rs. 150/ per month as compensation. The dispute between the parties related to the fixation of wages at Rs.150/ in the category of Draughtsmen and Rs. 100/ in case of other categories. The Tribunal held that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the new wage scales had been fixed with reference to the old wage scales and that the Tribunal was wrong in holding that the old wages scales were just and reasonable. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The award of the Industrial Tribunal is set aside and the workmen are entitled to get a flat increase of Rs. 250/ in their initial pay scale. [306G] 2. The new wage structure had been evolved by the Government for the purpose of fixing the wage scales. It was not possible to fix any higher wage scale on the basis of the old rates. The existing wage structure was not a mere device to reduce the existing wages and it could not be said that the increased wage scale was a device to increase the existing dearness allowance. [307H; 307A] 3. The revised wage scales having been fixed in the year 1973, there was no justification for increasing the existing rates of dearness allowance by increasing the basic pay of individual workmen. [308B] 4. The additional financial capacity as the Tribunal observed was not correct. It had to be borne in mind that the increase in the basic salary of individual workman was intended to apply to each individual workman, there is nothing in the body of the award to form the foundation on which the actual figures in the restructured pay scales can be made to rest. [309C] 5. The financial capacity of the workmen as a result of the original wage scales could not have been made to stand by the mere fact that they had already received some amount of additional financial liability. It is true that the award was made on December 20, 1978 but it was not made in the month of January, 1979. But it was made in July, 1980 and it was only after the award came into force that the workmen raised industrial disputes for revision of wage scales which were ultimately decided by the Tribunal on December 21, 1978. The basic idea underlying the original award was to give a flat increased wage structure to each workman. It could not therefore be said to have been intended to be a region or industry cum industry. [310E G] 6. The increase in dearness allowance is intended to cover both categories of Draughtsman and Rs., 100/ and Rs, 100/ respectively. The initial pay scales had necessarily to commence with figures Rs. 225/ and the basic wage had to start with figures at Rs 150/ and that was the one incorporated in the revised pay scales pertaining to different categories. [311G H] 7. The effect of the new award is that the wages of each workman would be fixed on entry into the service and resold without any additional financial benefit of salary. It cannot, therefore, be said, that the figure of Rs 150 was intended by the appellant. [312A B] 8.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1948. Its workmen were paid wages at the rate of Rs. 10/ per day and a piece of cloth was supplied to them by the respondent company. The company paid its employees only As. /10/ per month and that led to the present claim made by the respondents under section 15 of the Act. The appellant contended before the payment of wages authority that the refusal of the appellant to pay to them wages at rate awarded, in substance amounted to an illegal deduction from their wages and on that basis they asked for an order from the authority directing the appellant not to pay the wages. The authority did not decide the said question as a preliminary issue because it held that section 2(vi) included wages prescribed by the award. The Authority did not decided the said issue as a final one, but directed the appellant company to pay wages at rates fixed by the Industrial Tribunal. The respondents contended before this Court that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 10 of the , and that the claim of the respondents was barred by limitation. HELD: (i) The authority had found that section 3(vi)(a) included Wages prescribed by an award could not be included. [417 E] (ii) The provisions of section 2 (vi) are applicable to the case because, in reality, the wages prescribed under the award cannot fall within the definition prescribed by section 2.(vi). Therefore, it is difficult to accede to the argument that the wages prescribe by the Act can not be treated as wages under section 2. [420 G] (iii) The words "any award" and "any order" in section 2 of the Industrial Disputes Act are wide enough to include wages prescribed for any award. [416 A B] (iv) The definition of wages prescribed in an award cannot be construed as a contract between the parties because that, in truth, is the effect of industrial adjudication. That being so, it was difficult to subscribe to the contention that the wage prescribed by it could not fall within section 2,(vi). [418 C D] (v) The fact that on references made under section I 10(1) of the industrial Disputes Act, terms of employment have always been examined by industrial adjudication and wherever it appeared appropriate to make changes in them, they have been made in accordance with the well recognised principles of fair play and justice to both the parties.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department of Pepsu. He was prosecuted under section 409, Indian Penal Code and was convicted by the trial court. The High Court held that the prosecution had failed to establish an offence either under section 465 or section 409 of the Government of India Act, 1935, and that sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure was necessary for prosecuting him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the sanction under s. 197(l) of Code of criminal Procedure was not necessary for prosecution under section 120B, Indian penal Code and that the sanction was necessary only when the act complained of attached to the official character of the person doing it, and (ii) the trial was vitiated by non compliance with the provisions of section 197 (1) Of the Code. HELD : (i)(a) The sanction under sub s.(l) is not required for prosecution of a public servant under section409 or section 420 of the Indian Penal code. It is only when it is shown that the act alleged to have been done by the accused person while he was actually engaged in the performance of official duties, that the offence may be said to have taken place within the scope of his official duty if his act is such as to lie within the meaning of section 409 or section 465 of the Penal Code. [1305 D E] (b) The question whether sanction under sec. 197 (l) was necessary in a case falling within the purview of section 196(1), is one which falls squarely within the ambit of his duties and can be justified by him as done by virtue of his office. If sanction under that section is necessary, it would not be necessary to consider whether it is true or not is not a matter relevant at the stage of sanction but is not an issue between the prosecution and the accused. [1406 F G] (c) The provisions of s.197(l)(a), Cr. P.C., do not apply to cases where the official act complained against is directly concerned with his official duties so that, if questioned, it could be claimed to have done by him under the office, then sanction would be necessary; and that would be so irrespective of whether it was, in fact, a proper discharge of his duty. [1506 G H] (d) The section does not require that sanction should be obtained for prosecution against a public officer or servant who is concerned with the official duties. It only requires that sanction must be obtained by the authority concerned and not by the Government. [1607 B C] (e) The fact that the appellant did claim to have paid the amount to Parma, and the acquittance roll records the payment, and there was in acknowledgment thereof a thumb impression as against his name does not make any difference.

The appellant, a resident of Travancore State, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on the ground that it had been carrying on business in British India and its business in Travancore was not exempt from tax. The Income tax Officer held that the business losses incurred in the erstwhile State of Travancore were taxable as income under section 3 Of the Indian Incometax Act, and assessed the appellant to income Tax for the assessment year 1949 50. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer but the Tribunal held that it was not a case of total world income and therefore the business loss incurred in Travancore could be set off against the business profits made in the former State of Cochin. On reference, the High Court held that there was no question of any exemption from taxation under section 24(1) (Per Bose J.) that the appellant had been doing business in the territory of Travancore and that it did not carry on business as a business in India. Held, that the mere use of the words " loss of profits or gains" in section 24 (1) did not justify the construction that the intention of the Legislature was to restrict the set off of profits and losses arising in Indian States only to business or to modify the mode of computation under section 10 of the Indian Act. The mere fact that the word " income " is not used does not justify a construction that it would restrict the setting off of profit and loss arising in India only to businesses or to modification of the mode prescribed by sections 7 to 12B.

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1952 under which it had its registered office at Calcutta. The age of retirement for workmen in all industries should be 60 years subject to the employee passing a medical examination on reaching the age of 55. In September 1959 an agreement was entered into between the Company and its employees at Calcutta under which the age was extended to 58 years subject, inter alia, to 58. The company also agreed that the age shall be 60. The workmen 's case was that they were not entitled to any gratuity on the ground that they had been paid in the Bombay region. The Tribunal found that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns in Bombay region there was no uniform practice of fixing retirement at 60 years and that the trend was to fix the retirement age at 60. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The Tribunal has not committed any error in holding that the conclusion recorded by this Court in some of its earlier decisions as to the relevant trend in Bombay Region had been correct. [415 D] (ii) The award and agreements on the question of age of superannuation about which information is furnished by the several documents on this record clearly shows a consistent trend in the Madras region to fix retirement age of clerical and subordinate staff at 60, and the very few departures from this practice which the Tribunal has mentioned are wholly insufficient to indicate any slowing down of this trend. What was said by itself on an earlier occasion and was confirmed by this court in appeal, was in fact inaccurate. [427 G H] (iii) The awards and agreements have been made with a view to fix their retirement age for workmen at 60 and the award and agreement have also to be taken in this connection of the Report of the Norms Committee. [ 428 D E] (iv) The trend that has been expressed by the Tribunal in some cases is not very commendable, and that its present conclusion that what was said was wholly insufficient. What the Tribunal had failed to notice is that instances which may justify a revision of the judicial opinion expressed on an erroneous earlier occasion about a particular trend must be strong and unambiguous and they must speak for the period both before and more particularly after the previous finding had been recorded in the matter. [515 G H; 428 A] (v) The approach adopted by the Industrial Tribunal in dealing with this aspect of the problem is not quite correct. It has to be borne in mind that the Tribunal should take into consideration all the facts and circumstances disclosed by the oral and documentary evidence on this point, clearly show a consistent practice in the High Court to fix its retirement age.

The first respondent, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was appointed as the Chairman of the Board of Directors of the company. The first respondent filed an application before the Chairman for appointment of the second respondent as the chairman of the board of directors of the Company. The Chairman also stated that there were circumstances suggesting that the business of the appellant was being conducted with intent to defraud creditors, members and other persons and further that the persons concerned in the management of the affairs of the companies had in connection therewith been guilty of fraud, misfeasance and other misconduct towards the company and its members. The second respondent contended that the Board could not pass an order under section 237(b) of the Act as the first respondent was not a member of the first appellant company. Held: (i) The power conferred on the Central Government by section 237 (b) to order an investigation and delegated by it to the Company Law Board is administrative, that it could be validly exercised by the Chairman only if he had reason to believe that the circumstances suggest any of these things and not whether they establish any of those things. In the present case the first Respondent did not disclose anything from which it can be said that the inference which he has drawn was based on circumstances present before him. (ii) The Board was competent to delegate its function under section 236(b). The power to order investigation and delegation is administrative in character and that power cannot be delegated by the Board to itself. (iii) The powers conferred on a Chairman are administrative, and that it can only be validly exercise by an order made in pursuance of a rule enacted by the Central Govern ment under section 642(1) read with section 10E(5), that the exercise of the power does not violate any fundamental right of the appellants.

The appellants were tried and convicted for the same offence and received a like sentence. The High Court confirmed their conviction but reduced the sentence to three years rigorous imprisonment. In appeal by special leave, it was contended that the presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Act had not been drawn since the circumstances did not admit the drawing of such a presumption in the case, according to the prosecution, and therefore the appellants were themselves the dacoits. HELD : The High court was right in holding that the appellants had failed to establish their complicity in the crime of dacoity and therefore they could be convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code. [724 D] In the present case the goods stolen were a large quantity of cloth taken for sale to the market. These goods were not sold and were being taken back to the dealers by the cartmen. The appellants had been rightly convicted under sections 395 and 412 of the I.P.C. [700 E F] The High 'Court was right that the sentence of three years ' rigorous imprisonment should be reduced to one year 's rigorous imprisonment, but not of fine. [624 G H] In this case the appellants did not have any explanation for their having committed the offence of dacoity. They were merely receivers of stolen property from some other 20 persons who were the dacoits and had looted the property. The house of 20 persons was searched and large quantities of cloth were found in their houses. It is difficult to think that within the short time available, these goods could have been easily disposed of to receivers of theft or could be placed in the custody of friends till such time as the original offenders could take them away.

The petitioners, who were manufacturers of 'thinner ' in the country, filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for issue of a writ of mandamus directing the State Government to include in the list of substances included in the Rules as "poppy arsenic" and enabled State Government, by Rule 13 thereof, to declare any substance as poison for the purposes of the Act. The petitioners contended that since the Act is a Central enactment it is possible of unjust and unjustified discriminatory treatment as it is left to each State Government not to determine what substance they would include as poison and regulated and the decision in one State to include the substance as medicine was not automatically made applicable to other States. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The object of the enactment is to regulate the importation, possession and sale of poisons. Some substances were included in it. The Act is intended to regulate its import, possession, sale and disposal of poisonac in which the use of such poison for purposes of committing murder or mischief by poisoning cattle appears to be of such frequent occurrence as to render restriction on the posses sion thereof desirable. If the Government thought in the circumstances that the possi sion or sale of the same is to be regulated it could not be said that they have no power to regulate. [222C D] 2. The expression "polysenic", the expanded words are used in a sense similar to those used in the Act, and the object of which is to control the poss ession thereof desirable, is to render provision for regulating the possession of any specified poison in any local area in which it is intended for use as an ingredient of murder or other offence. [223D E] 3. The purpose of the legislation is to ensure that the possession and disposal in the State is not restricted to the quantity of poison and consequential amendment of rules 12 and 13 of the Rules. [225E F] 4. The notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity to declare the substance which it considers to be poison for purpose of committing death or mischief, by poisoning. If Government thought that the possess ment or sale was to be governed in the interest of health and safety of the society, it could have no such power to control. [226F G] 5. The Notification and its appli cation to any other area would not depend on necessity to declaring the substance ance as poison. [227G] 6. The Government may by rule regulate the import, Possession and sale or sale to be regulating the possibil ity for sale or disposal of the specified poison. It is in exercise of this power Rule 13 was amended by substituting the old Rule by following Rule 13. [228H; 227A B] 7. The State Government may, by rule regulating the import or possession of potions, possession etc., which shall be kept within such box, almirah, room or building in a separate closed receptacle of glass, metal and earthenware etc. The nature of trade in poison is such that nobody can be considered to have an absolute right to carry on the same. [229C D; 228D] 8. The notifications and the application to the any area will depend on whether the substance was specified as a poison or not. If it is found that the Government has no power under the Act to regulate, the possession for sale and the sale of such an article would be governed by Rule 12. [230E F; 228F] 9.

The assessee firm was carrying on business at Madras in drugs, chemicals, mercury, camphor and silk yam and as money lenders. The assessee firm applied to the Tribunal for a statement of case on the following question: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the Tribunal was right in holding that the debt of Rs. 2,68,385/ written off by the assessee in their books of account as irrecoverable in the books of accounts was not one incurred in the course of money lending business of the assessee ?" The High Court answered the question in favour of the Department and against the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that: (1) the debt was not a bad and doubtful debt in its money lending, and (2) the Tribunal had erred in disallowing the claim of the appellant for the balance of Rs 2, 68,385. HELD : (i) The Tribunal has found that the monies were not loans made in the ordinary course of business of appellants ' firm. [10 E] (ii) The finding of the Tribunal is binding on this Court and it cannot be said that the Tribunal erred in allowing the claim for the entire amount of Rs, 2,69,385 as a bad debt. [11 D] (iii) The expression "accommodation" has been defined in section 10(2)(xi) to mean any building or part of a building which is used principally for residential purposes and includes any accommodation intended for residential or other purposes. The word 'accommodations ' has not been defined either in the Act or in the Rules made thereunder. [12 E] In the present case, the Tribunal has held that the amounts were not loan advanced by the appellant to the Bombay firm. It is true that the amount was paid to the assessee as loan and it was not shown that the said amount was borrowed for a purpose other than money lending. But the fact that the assessee had made an application to the tribunal under section 66(1) of the Income tax Act, 1922 to submit a statement on the question "whether on the circumstances and in its circumstances of this case the disallowance of the bad debt of the Rs.2,68.385 was justified in law" does not mean that the debts were not advanced in the normal course of the money lending or that they were not repaid by the Bombay Firm. [13 E F] (iv) The tribunal has found on facts that the moneys sent by the respondent to the High firm were not ' loans made for the purpose of advancing the financial crisis, threatening it in Samvat Year 2007, and that the transactions were totally unconnected with the normal business of their firm. The Tribunal had found that monies sent by them were not debts owed to the appellant.

The petitioners were owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of the Bangalore Development Act, 1976. The Land Acquisition (Amendment) Act, 1984 was brought into force on September 20, 1977. The petitioners obtained an interim order from this Court directing status quo with regard to the possession of the lands in question in Special Leave Petition No. 294 of 1985 preferred against the said order of the High Court dated August 14, 1984. The said special leave petition was dismissed by a Division Bench of that High Court on April 29, 1987. In these two writ petitions, the petitioners challenged the acquisition on the ground that they were not made within two years of the notification making the declaration under section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. Dismissing the Special Leave Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The fact of the stay orders was highly material in the determination of these Special Leave petitions. [565E] 2. The question whether the awards were made within the stipulated time or not is a matter which has to be decided by the court on the basis of the evidence and materials placed before it. [567F] 3. In the instant case, the respondents have failed to make out any case for interference with the acquisition proceedings. [568G] 4. The Special Leave Petitioners are approaching this Court for such relief must come with clean hands. They have not approached this Court with clean hand and they have not suppressed material facts. [569F] 5. The High Court has granted interim stay of dispossession in respect of the said lands. It is well settled that the relief under Article 136 of the Constitution is discretionary and a petitioner who approaches this Court seeking such relief should come with frank and full disclosure of facts. If he fails to do so and suppresses material facts, his application is liable to be dismissed. [570F] 6. The order granting interim stay is not a direction for continuance of the proceedings till the disposal of the Special leave petition. It does not amount to suppression of material facts or there was no concealment of material fact. [571G H] 7. The petitioner has failed to show that the stay order was made within time. If the respondents appeared in response to the notice and filed their counter affidavit, they have failed in their defence. They are liable to pay compensation for the delay caused by them. [573F G] 8.

The appellant, a workman in the respondent Bank, was appointed as an Assistant Manager on January 1, 1959. He was drawing basic pay at Rs. 400 per month and was getting a salary of Rs. 100 per month. The appellant 's services were terminated by the respondent bank with effect from January 1. 1962. The respondent bank filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the termination of his services. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the workman had not been given any opportunity to show cause against the action proposed to be taken against him and that he was entitled to increments under sub cl. (b) of cl. 100 of the Sastry award. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent was not given an opportunity to explain his conduct before terminating his services and that the termination was illegal as the workman did not give any opportunity of being heard before terminating the services of the respondent. HELD: (i) The respondent Bank had no right to terminate the services without giving any opportunity for showing cause against termination of service. [901 B] (ii) The appellant had no power to terminate his services after he had been given an adequate opportunity of hearing. [936 C] (iii) The procedure prescribed by cl. 2(b) and (c) of para 5 of the award was not followed. [951 D] (iv) The principle that a workman should be given an effective opportunity of showing cause is applicable only where there is no specific provision in the statute or in the rules for the termination or discharge of his service. In the present case, the respondent had been afforded an adequate and reasonable opportunity to defend himself. [948 E] (v) The principles laid down by this Court in the case of National Industrial Tribunal, Bombay vs K. M. Desai, ; , applied. (vi) The award was valid because it did not contain any provision for giving a hearing to the respondent before terminating or discharging his services nor did it specify any particular procedure for the same. [947 G] (vii) The provisions of para. 5(b), (c), (d) and sub cl.(iv) of el. (a) of the Award were not complied with.

The appellant, a resident of Calcutta, was granted a lease of the land to the Taj Group of Hotels for the construction of a Five Star Hotel. The lease deed provided that the lessee shall not assign or transfer any right in the site or any part thereof without the previous consent of the Government. The appellant applied for a lease and obtained an order from the Government of West Bengal, but the same was refused on the ground that it had been granted by the Government under section 3(1) of the . The appellant challenged the said order before the High Court in a writ petition which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the decision to lease the Begumbari land to Taj Group was taken on February 12, 1981; (ii) the Government had no power to grant four acres of Begumbar land to any person other than the Taj group of Hotels; and (iii) the order of the State Government was not in accordance with law. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The decision to grant 4 acres of the Begum land to a Taj Group is taken on March 12,1981. It is on a total evaluation of various considerations which have weighed with the Government in taking a particular action, that the Court would have to decide whether the action of the Govern ment was reasonable and in public interest. [260F] 2. The purpose of the grant of four acres is to start with the construction industry and to provide for the establishment of industries within the State. It has been provided by the Act that the Government shall take steps to establish industries within its jurisdiction, and if so required, the Government may issue a notification in the Official Gazette specifying the areas which would be included in the area for the purpose of this Act. [261F] 3. The object of the Act is to provide a machinery for the regulation of the development of the area and for the prevention of exploitation of land by the State or for any other purposes connected with the development thereof. It also provides that the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 shall apply to all proceedings under the Act. The Act has been enacted in order to protect the interests of the people of India. [262G H] 4. The Government was quite alive to the need for expanse of the zoo. The proposed hotel is a Garden Hotel and there is perhaps every chance of the ecology and environment improving as a result of planting several trees all around the proposed hotel and the removal of the burial ground and burning ground for rubbish. [263A] 5. The State has made available to this court all documents in connection with the proposal for lending over a piece of land to respondent No. 1. It was on a consideration of all the facts and circumstances that the State had made available all documents, in connection therewith, to the appellant. The matter was taken in appeal. [264B] 6. The High Court has not properly appreciated the evidence and has committed an error in holding that the land which was undoubt edly Government land, to start a Five star hotel, was given to the Tolaram for construction of five Star Hotel in Calcutta. The land allotted to the hotel was, as it was not used for the main purpose of building a Fivec Star hotel. [265C] 7. The question whether the land is required for the project or not has to be decided on the basis that the purpose for which the land was acquired would interfere with the animal in the Zoo. [267E F] 8.

The assessee, a Hindu Undivided Family, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1957 58. The assessee claimed that the sum of Rs.67,560/12/ was wrongly included in the net wealth of the assessee. The Income Tax Officer rejected this claim on the ground that the assessee did not make valid gifts aggregating Rs.1 lakh on 1.1.1957 and Rs.50,000 on 31.1 .1957. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the amount of Rs,67,561/12 was rightly included in its net wealth. The Tribunal, however, held that there was no valid gift of the said amount and that the High Court had erred in answering the question in favour of the Revenue. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant assessee that the view taken by the High Courts in New India citation is correct. On behalf of respondent assessee it was submitted that the decision of the Delhi High Court in New Indian feature Co. vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Delhi, was not applicable to the facts and circumstances of the case. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in answering question in the manner it did. [130C] 2. In the instant case, the assessee had made a valid gift and trust in respect of the amount gifted could not be held to have been validly made by debiting the assessee 's personal account in the books of the Hindu undivided family with Rs. 50,000 and crediting the same in the personal account of his son. [131D] 3. The question whether there was a valid gifts or trust in the hands of the donee and gift in such case will not be valid. [132E] 4. In view of the fact that the entries in the accounts of the family were made contemporane ously shown to be fictitious, it resulted in a valid transfer of the shares of the donees by debit ing the assessee"s personal Account in the names of the minor donees and the amount was available to that firm or the company or H.U.F. on the date of gift, then a valid Gift by book entries might be possible but where a sum was not available with the firm or family or a company which was not a banking company or which had no overdraft facility, by mere book entries even though there was acceptance of that gift by the donee would not effectuate a valid gifted. [133F G] 5. The fact that a sum of money was not received in cash or in any other form with a bank or with a banking Company and that amount is available to the firm for being kept in the account of the father does not constitute a valid sale. [134G H] 6. In order to decide whether there is a valid receipt or trust, it is necessary to consider the nature of the gift as well as the source from which it was made. The test is whether the donor has received the money and the property is properly gifted or not. If the donor had received the amount in cash, he would have been able to get it back with the money. [135A B] 7. In a case where the assessee has a credit balance with firm or with family or with any banking company and that sum is available for being used by the firm, or the firm as a banking institution or which has no overdraft facilities by mere books entries even if there was accepted gift by him would not subserve a valid transaction. [136C D] 8. In such cases, the question whether the assessee received the amounts in cash and the balance of Rs 50, 000 is available with that firm to be kept in its account in a bank. [137E F] 9. The amount of the donor was not liable to be included in property passing on the death of M.

The appellant was a member of the Orissa High Court and was posted as Superintendent and legal remembrance. The High Court held that Shri B.K. Patro, district and sessions judges were not competent to act as law secretary, superintendent and legal person in charge of administrative posts as District Judges. The State Government issued an order dated October 10, 1966 directing the Chief Secretary to the Government of Orissa to send back judicial officers working in administrative posts to the cadre of district judges or as addl district judges as the case may be after they had held those posts for three years or more. On November 10, 1967 the High Court directed that the appellant should be posted as superintendent and Legal remembrancer in March 1962. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the order of the High. Court on the ground that he was not competent under article 233 to act on the basis of the order dated November 10 1966. The petition was dismissed by the High, Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the order passed by the State Government holding that those officers had no authority to hold the posts in question is unsustainable; and (2) the High 'Court was not justified in posting Shri BK. Sen as the law secretary to the government of Orissa, the Home Secretary to Government of India, the Chief Minister to the Govern ment of Orissa and the Home Secretaries to the State Governments, the Secretary to Governor, the Finance Department, the Director General of Police, the Deputy Inspector General of Prisons, the Superintendent of Police and the District Magistrate, who were members of the executive committee constituted under article 235 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1)(a) The High ' Court was not right in posting the appellant as the Law Secretary to government of the State. [517 B] (b) The order of transfer dated October 1, 1966 is unsustainable. The Government has already implemented that part of the Order as well. In the result these appeals are partly allowed and the order quashing the order posting Shri K.B. Panda as superintendent is set aside. [525 C D] (2)(a). The High court was right in holding that the orders posting Shri P.C. Sen were not valid. [500 E] (3) The Government had already implemented the part of its order as well as the other directions issued by it from time to time.

The appellants, who were the sons of the vendor and vendors, filed a suit for pre emption against the respondent on the ground that they had purchased under tenan cy of the sale deed dated 10.12.1954 executed by their father in favour of the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit holding that there was no infringement of Article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution and that there were no infringement or infringement of article 19(i)(f). On appeal, the High Court held that there had been no infringement and that the appellants had failed to prove their case. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that since the suit land belonged to more than one co sharer and had not been sold jointly by all the co sharers, he as a co shar holder could claim pre empt of the right of pre emment conferred on him by that provision. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The object of the Act is to provide for the better regulation of sale and purchase of agricultural land in the State. Section 15(1) (a) provides that where a sale is of a share out of joint land or property, and is not made by all co sharists jointly, only the other co sharen ters and the tenants can exercise the right to pre empators. [127F G] 1.2 The object is to confer the right on specified family members of the vendors of the land or properties sold or a part thereof. It is not possible to lay down any general rule that the legislature intended to confer such a right on certain persons as co sharants. [128B C] 1:3. In the instant case, the suit lands belonged to several co sharators and had been purchased by all of them. The appellants were not in possession of the co co shar er or vendors of other co co co share.

The father of the appellant, who was a minor, executed a will in respect of certain properties in favour of his two sons and the same was registered on 21.8.1987. The said deed provided that the petitioner would pay Rs. 1 lakh to each of his three sons in lieu of relinquishment of their interest. On 21.9.1987, the father and his two brothers executed a compromise whereby they agreed to pay Rs 1 lakh each to each one of them in lieu thereof. The petitioner 's mother died on 22.8 .1987. In view of the said compromise, the petitioner filed an application for execution of the decree. On 20.9 .1987, when the matter was listed before the Court for recording of the compromise, Sudarshan Gupta, second respondent, maintained that he had not been paid Rs.1 lakh as stipulated and he had no intention to accept the compromise. The Court passed a decree on 22nd September, 1987 in terms of the aforesaid compromise. On 30th April, 1991, the appellant filed an execution petition for realisation of the amount due from him. The first respondent filed an objection stating that the said alienations were valid and binding on the petitioner and that the alienees had no interest in the property to part with in view of clause (a) of the consent decree. The executing Court rejected the objection and passed a preliminary decree for Rs.77,124 being the amount paid by the father to each other. The High Court dismissed the revision petition filed by the petitioner. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the alienations were invalid as they had been made in violation of the terms of compromise and that there was no valid consent of one of the parties to the compromise and the sale deeds were subsequent to 21. 8 1987, and therefore the sale transactions were void ab initio. On behalf of respondent No. 2 it was submitted that the alienation was valid and the transferees had become owners of the property and had even maintained that there had been improvements of the properties by the alienee. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have rightly held that once the Court was satisfied that there is a compromise it was for the Court to record the same and no option lay before the court to act otherwise. [541C] 1.2 In view Of the fact that there were allegations of payment of Rs. l lakh to the petitioner, which too was not investigated and to meet the further allegation that some improvements have been made to the property which too is not in dispute, it is directed that the sale shall be disposed of and the terms and conditions of the agreement shall form part of the order to be drawn up in this Court for disposing of the special leave petition. [542D] 1:3. The amount paid as stipulated by the compromise shall stand discharged and the alienors will have no liability to account for mesne profits. [543E] 1 Whether or not the alienation is valid and whether the transferees have become owners thereof, is a question of fact to be decided on the basis of evidence led before the trial court. The parties are directed to appear before the executing Court on 30th of April,1991. If necessary, the Trial Court may appoint a Commissioner and take police help for executing this order and such cost shall ultimately be borne by the defaulting alienees but may initially be met by Seshiah.

The appellant company was entitled to sickness benefit for the first two days of sickness except in the case of a spell of sickness following at an interval of not more than 15 days, the spell of sick leave. The workmen were not entitled to the sickness benefit under the Act. The Tribunal held that the benefits admissible under the provisions of the Act in the matter of grant of sick Leave are such as to justify the rejection of the workmen 's demand and set aside the award in that respect. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the benefit of sick leaves should be granted only in the cases of sickness certified by a registered medical practitioner and not otherwise. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The Tribunal has rightly examined the matter and given adequate reasons for allowing the benefit to the workmen. [84E] (2) The Industrial Tribunal has taken into consideration all aspects of the demand for sickness benefit and did not take into account all aspects including the adequacy of the sick leave for which sickness benefit was last paid. It is true that the Tribunal has examined the controversy and given sufficient reasons for disallowing the benefit. But it cannot be said that the award is vitiated by any error apparent on the face of the record. [85F G] (3) The expression "any other matter" in section 49 of the , does not mean anything more than what is expressly stated therein. It means something more than mere arithmetical mistake or an error which is apparent on a plain reading of the award. [86G H; 86A] (4) The word "dispute" has been used in the widest possible terms to include all matters which are capable of being referred to arbitration. The expression 'disputes ' has not been defined in the Act and it is only when a dispute arises that the matter can be referred for adjudication by an arbitrator or arbitrators. [87G H] (5) The award in the instant case was made effective from January 1, 1975. It was not necessary to award the benefit under section 49 in the matters of grant or additional privilege leave for 7 days in the garb of sick and sickness.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1) of the Bombay Prevention of Dangerous Activities of Bootleggers, Drug Offenders and Dangerous Activities Act, 1958. The grounds furnished to him were that he had been indulging in various activities prejudicial to the maintenance of public order and that he was carrying on espionage activities which were prejudicial to public order. He challenged his detention by a petition under article 226 of the Constitution on the ground that (1) the detaining authority had not given him the opportunity of making a representation against the order, (2) the grounds supplied to him did not disclose any particulars of the activities alleged to have been carried on by him and (3) the impugned order was mala fide. The High Court dismissed the petition. Held, that the grounds furnished were vague or not in the sense that they were vague. The ground supplied was not vague or did not indicate the source from which it could be inferred. The power of detention can be exercised only if there is a clear and cogent material to show that the person concerned had been acting in a manner prejudicial to maintenance of law and order. In the present case, the grounds were not vague nor did they contain any particulars as to how the activities of the petitioner were alleged to be prejudicial to "public order". The grounds supplied were not such as would justify the inference that the detaining author ity was acting in an arbitrary manner or in a casual manner. The right of the detenue to be furnished particulars under article 22(5) to the extent of denying all particulars and leaving the grounds absolutely vague is not a fundamental right. The order of detention cannot be sustained by reason of the claim in public interest of non disclosure of facts made by the Under Secretary to the Government of Bombay by means of his affidavit filed in the High Court.

The respondent was a member of the General Court Martial. He was dismissed from service by an order dated September 9, 1959. The Central Government directed removal from service under r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954. On April 9, 1960, the Chief of the Military Staff passed an order removing him from service. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal on the ground that r.14 was ultra vires the , and that the action taken thereunder was without authority. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that r 14 was ultra rites as it was not ultra vires. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Rule 14 is a self contained code and does not offend article 14 of Constitution. [449 B] (ii) The words "subject to the provisions of this Act" in r. 15 are wide enough to include within its ambit the power to remove an officer from the service. Rule 14 was therefore ultra vires as it contravened articles 14 and 16 of the Constitu tion. [445 C D] (iii) The word "subject" in section 19 makes it clear that there should be rules, and subject to the provision of the Act and such rules, the Central Government may dismiss or remove from the Service any person subject to this Act. [453 E] (iv) Rule 15 is a general rule which deals with punishment for misconduct against an officer whose further retention in service is not considered desirable. The words 'subject to this provision ' occurring in section 191 make it clear of the intention of the legislature that there must be rules and subject thereto, the central Government has been given the power under r, 14 to dismiss or removal from the serv ice any person. [454 G] (v) Rule 16 is a special rule which provides for punishment for unbecoming conduct, viz., section 45. The two sections 19 and 45 are mutually exclusive. They deal with the procedure for imposing penalties. Rule 15 deals with dismissal or removal of an officer who has been dismissed from the services. Rule 16(1) does not contain any specific provision for punishment.

The appellant company was carrying on the business of manufacturing tea. The Government of Bombay issued a notification under section 3(1) of the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901, exempting the factory from octroi duty for consumption, use or sale. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the notification was invalid because it did not specify the rate at which it was to be levied and that the Government had no power under section 23(1)(a) of Bombay District Municipalities Act, 1922, to levy octroi duty on tea imported into the Panchayat limits for consumption use or sold. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The notification issued by the Government did not contain any provision requiring the Panchayat to notify to the public not only the proposal about the tax selected by it for levy but also the rules relating to that tax which must mean the action taken under the Act and the rules. [218 E] The word "may" in section 23 (1)(b) of that Act, does not mean that the Panchayat should have the power to impose octroi duty. It is only when a panchayat finally decides to levy any tax or fee that it can impose the tax or fees. [282 F G] The words "any tax or tax" in the section are wide enough to include all taxes and fees which may be imposed by the Panchayat for consumption or sale, and the word "tax" in this section means a tax or a tax. [220 C D] The Government was entitled to deal with the appeal on merits.

The appellant No. 1 was employed in the respondent company as a driver and proceedings were taken on a complaint by the Conciliation Officer under section 33 read with section 31(1) of the , against the appellants. The conciliation proceedings commenced at the instance of the appellant No 1 and the conciliation proceedings were held on December 13, 1951, but the conciliation proceeding was not concluded within 14 days of the commencement of the conciliation Proceedings or within such shorter period fixed by the appropriate Government. The respondent filed a complaint before the Conciliation officer under section 31 read with sections 33 and 33(1). The appellants contended that as the conciliation had continued for a period of more than 14 days as from January 17, 1952, further proceedings for conciliation were illegal and therefore the accused persons could not be convicted under section 30(1), read with s.33(1); Held, that the conciliation was not completed within 14th day of the date fixed by Government under section 12(6) of Act and the proceedings were not concluded on December 31, 1951. The provisions of the Act do not apply to the proceedings before the conciliation officer as they are not commenced after January 17. 1952, but when that report is received by the State Government it cannot be said that the proceedings did not commence until January 17; but if for some reason the Conciliation Officers delay the submission of his report, their action (1) ; , , followed. The Act provides for commencement and conclusion of conciliation proceedings under section 20 but the first sub section of section 20 deals with what are called utility services and sub section 2 of that section provides as to when the conciliation shall conclude. Section 20(2)(b) provides that the report of the Conciliation Offi cer shall be submitted by the conciliation Officer within 14 day from the date on which the proceeding is pending. The first sub sec tion of section 12 contemplates the submission by the Government or the Advisory Board, and the second sub sec tions of section 13 deal with what were called utility service and sub secti on (2) of that sub section provides for the commencement and termination of conciliation proceeding under section 21. The second sub section deals with the manner in which the conciliation is concluded and the third sub secre sion of section 15 deals with cases where no settlement is reached, when the report is made by the Board. The third sub section (2)(a) provides for an appeal to the State Govt. against any order of the Tribunal or the National Tribunal. The appellant No 2 was appointed as a workman in the first respondent company on January 17 and the Conciliation proceedings were pending at the time when the Conciliation Act came into force. The Conciliation Officer submitted his report under section 13(6). The conciliation proceeding therefore did not end when the second respondent made his report. The State Government held that the Conciliation Proceedings could be prolonged for a long period as the first subsection of section 18 of the said Act contemplates the filing of the report by the Advisory Committee within 14 working days of March 18, 1952 and if proceedings were closed, as provided in section 20(1)(b), the termination would depend upon how soon a report is submitted to the appropriate Govern ment. The contention that the first substi tution was not commenced before January 17 was rejected by the High Court.

The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the , on the ground that he was a member of an unlawful assembly and was likely to be enlarged on bail. The grounds stated that there was indiscriminate firing between two rival groups, and that the petitioner had disturbed the normal tempo of life in Katras and Jogta Police Station. The detaining authority after considering all the relevant factors, passed the order of detention. The petitioner challenged the order by filing a writ petition before the High Court which dismissed it. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order was made on one incident relating to exchange of fire between two groups and that there were no materials for passing the order, and therefore the detention was illegal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of preventive detention passed by the respondent no.1 is set aside. [910C] 2. In a case where the actual order of release was served upon the detenu, the detenu was in jail. There is no indication that this factor or the question that the said detenu might be released or that there Was such a possibility of his release, was taken into consideration by the detaining authority properly and seriously before the service of the order. [099D] 3. The detention order was set aside on the sole ground that the detenu 's activities were prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. It is not stated that this fact or the questions that the detaining authoritY had given any opportunity to the detenu to explain his position. If that is the position, then however, it is inconceivable that the antecedents of a person might have been without consideration of all the aforesaid relevant factors. [109E F] Rameshwar Shaw vs District Magistrate Burdwan & Anr., ; , referred to.

The respondent firm, manufacturers of gold and silver, was manufacturing gold. The firm had a stock in the name of its partners. In the year 1965, the firm purchased gold from the firm. The stock in trade was found to be more than Rs. 1 lac. The Income Tax Officer assessed the firm as a dealer under section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of assessment and held that the firm had failed to prove its case against it. In further revision, the High Court set aside the order holding that the assessee was not entitled to any relief on the ground of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred upon him thereunder could be exercised by the Administrator but that is not decisive of the matter. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts ' decision in unamended sec. 28 of 1968 has resulted from excessive delegation and that the provisions of section 28 are violative of article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as the power to grant or renew a license to a dealer is not absolute but conditional upon the Administrator having regard to the policy and purpose of the Act, and by reference thereto, the power is conferred on him. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The objective of putting the Act on the Statute Book as indicated by its long title is "to provide in the economic and financial interests of the community", for the control of production, manufacture, supply, distribution, use and possession of and business in gold ornaments and articles of gold. [955C] 1.2 In the absence of any specific provision in the Act or the scheme of the enactment providing sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section, it is not obligatory upon him to exercise his discretion in the manner he has done. The purpose and object of the statute is to ensure prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the Acts in making his orders. [936D] 1:3. In order to be a valid law, it must be made by the legislature with the object of promoting the interest of the general public. It does not impose any blanket or absolute prohibition upon a dealer from carrying on money lending, banking or any other business in the same premises in which he carries on business as a dealers but he is prevented only from carrying out his obligations under that Act in making such orders. The object and purpose underlying the enactment and the scheme are to ensure speedy disposal of cases by the authorities concerned. [951E F] 1 :4. In view of the fact that the legislature has not provided for any criteria or guidelines for guiding the discretion of the Administrator, it cannot be struck down on the grounds of excessive delegations of legislative powers. [953F G] 1 5. The objective is to provide in economic and industrial interests of a class of persons who are engaged in business as dealers but they are prevented only by the authority of law from carrying them out their duties in accordance with the provisions contained in the statute. [948G H; 949A] 1 6. The scheme of Gold Control as envisaged by the Act together with the necessity to ensure protection of the interest and the policy of the Central Government shall not be premitted. [949B C] 1 7. The Administrator is required to have regard to all the policy, purposes and purposes of the , in making its orders. He may also delegate his powers under section 5(1) of the . [948C D] 2.1 In the instant case, the various provisions of Gold control Act, 1969 show that the Administrator was required to exercise the power of granting or renewing a license for a dealer. The only restriction imposed by the Section is that the unamended sec tion for the purpose of granting and renewing a licence to a dealers should be in economic, financial and educational interests.

The appellants were the owners of agricultural lands situated in Eragudi village, Musiri Taluk. The suit was filed by the respondents against four respondents claiming that they were entitled to the possession of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit and the first appellate Court found that the title of the alienees in regard to 'dharmadlayam properties had not been acquired by adverse possession before the suit was instituted, but it held that the appellants had acquired title by adverse posses sion prior to 1 1 1929. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decision of the first Appellate Court and restored the decree passed by the trial court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question as to whether a transfer effected by the manager of a temple in regard tO 'dharnam properties had been acquired or not was a mixed question of fact and law, and the High Courts were right in reversing the decisions of the courts below by holding that title of an alienee in regard of 'dharmam properties could not be lost if his predecessor who made the transfer lives for more than 12 years after effecting the transfer. [866 D] (ii) The fact that the alienor was still alive and so, it thought that the plea of adverse possession could not he sustained must necessarily imply that the transfer was effected by him as manager. [886 E F] (iii) The High Court was in error in reversing decisions of courts below on the findings recorded by the courts. [881 G] (iv) The contention that the question as regards title of ' Karanmadlukayam properties could be raised only before the trial Court and not before the High court, cannot be accepted. The question whether a particular property belonged to the manager or not must depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [ 867 D] Gnanasambanda vs H. C. Bhari, A.I.R. , referred to. (v) The finding recorded by courts below that the transferor and his family had been performing the worship of the temple for the past 27 years was not challenged in this Court.

The appellant firm was carrying on the business of cinema business in the State of Jammu and Kashmir. The licence for exhibition of cinematographs in the building known as Apsara Theatre, Gandhi Nagar, Jammu was granted by the District Magistrate in favour of the firm. The firm applied to the District Magis trate for a renewal of the licence. The District Magistrate rejected the request on the ground that the licence had been granted to the firm and that it had become impossible for him to operate the Cinema licence in view of the temporary injunction issued by the High Court. The appellant filed an appeal before the State Government against the order of the District magistrate. The State Government dismissed the appeal holding that the renewal of a licence could not be made in the name of any party other than the original licensee, namely, the licensee, who had been declared to be the sole licensee in respect of the Apsar Theatre by the proceedings of his predecessor dated December 29, 1977 which was confirmed in appeal by the State Govt. and which had acquired finality between the parties by reason of the dismissal of the writ petition and the Special Leave Petition by the appellant. The High Court dismissed the writ appeal filed by the firm against the orders of the Sub Divisional Magistrate. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the licensing authority had no power under the Act or the Rules to suspend a licence which could be made only in the names of the original licensees, namely the licensee and there was no mention at all of the partners of the Firm or its partners. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order passed by the Sub Divnt Magistrate directing the suspension of cinema shows in the Theatre cannot be said to have visited the writ petitioners with any adverse civil consequences. [578F] 2. The licensing authority has no power to suspend the licence which can be made under section 6 F of the Act as one implicit in the larger power of revocation and unless the conditions precedent mentioned in the section are present, the licensing authori ty had no jurisdiction to suspend it. [579A B] 3. The only reason stated by the high Court for quashing the District Commissioner 's order is that the District Magistrates had no authority under the . Act or Rules to make such an order. [580C D] 4. The power to suspended a licence is conferred only by section 6F of the , as one implied in the wider power of revoking and unless there is any provision in the Act, the rules framed thereunder cannot be deemed to have been repealed. [581D] 5. The mere fact that the licensee has been declared an insolvent or a person holding an office under him does not by itself make him a party to the proceedings for due compliance with all the terms and conditions of the license and answerable to the licensing authorities for all commissions and omissions in the cinema premises. [583E F] 6.

The appellants, who were the owners of certain properties in Pakistan, entered into an agreement with the respondent for the purchase of certain mills and factory in question. The terms of the agreement were that the mills would be leased to them for a period of five years on the terms and conditions set out therein. On 12 2 1954 the respondent issued a notice to the appellants under section 12 of the Act, terminating the lease. The appellants challenged the validity of the notice by filing a petition in the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that section 12 was ultra vires the powers of the Custodian and set aside the order of termination. On appeal by certificate, Held, that section 10 Of the Act did not apply to leases granted by the evacuee and not by the Custodian himself. The provisions of section 10 of the Bombay Act were applicable only to leases issued by the evacuees and not to leases executed by them. The words "any lease" in section 12 meant a transfer of property made for consideration and not for any other purpose. The word "transfer" in the context means a transfer for consideration, and therefore, it could not be said that the Custodian had no power under section 10 to cancel the lease granted by himself. It was not correct to say that the words "by the evacuee" in s.12 were intended to include a transfer made for valuable consideration. The effect of the sale was that the property was transferred to the evacuee, and the property could be sold only if it was found that there was no valid contract between the parties. The Custodian had the power under s.10 to cancel a lease granted in favour of the appellants, but he did not do so. The right of the appellant to cancel an agreement to sell the mills and the factory to them was not affected by section 10. The rights of the parties were left open to the determination of the appropriate authorities, and that nothing in the Act should be taken as a pronouncement on those rights.

The appellant was a minor son of the respondent. The Sub Divisional Officer, Hanumangarh, by his order dated 5th May, 1976 determined the ceiling area but an appeal by Raghubir Singh to the Revenue Appellate Authority was dismissed on March 6, 1973 and the Board of Revenue set aside the order of the Sub Divisional officer on March 7, 1973. The appellant filed a revision application before the Board which allowed the same and remanded the case to the Sub Divi sion Officer Hanumangadha, who by his orders dated 5.5.1976 directed that the ceiling should be determined according to old law i.e. Act of 1955 and not according to new law i954. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court which was allowed by the Board on March 12, 1973 holding that it was not correct to say that section 9 is limited to the executive control and superintendence of the Board over subordinate revenue courts and it does not apply to judicial proceedings. The High Court also held that it is not correct for the Board to exercise the powers conferred by Section 9 of the land Revenue Act in view of the fact that the Board had appellate jurisdiction and it could not, therefore, make use of its powers of superintendence and control and the order passed by the Sub divisional Officer was illegal. The State filed a special leave petition against the judgment of the High court. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. Section 222 of the Act of 1956 is similar to section 107 of the Government of India Act, 1915 and there is no section like sub section (2) of Section 224 of the Govern ment of India. [726C] 2. The Board of revenue has general powers of supervision over all revenue courts. In the Government it has general power of superintendence over all Revenue Courts. It does not affect any judgment of any inferior court which was not otherwise subject to appeal or revision. [ 727D] 3. Section 221 of the , is similar in nature to section 108 of the Govt. of India, Act, 1935 and there are no sections like sub sections (2), 107 of Government ofIndia Act, 1913 in the Act.

The first respondent, the Chief Controller of Sales Tax, was appointed as an Assistant Commissioner of Sales tax in the State of Orissa. The first respondent was appointed by the Central Government as a Sales Tax Officer on ad hoc basis for a period of two years. He was later promoted as Additional Sales Tax officer. In the year 1973 he was served with a notice under section 9(2) of the Act calling upon him to show cause why he should not be called upon to pay the tax due from him. The second respondent challenged the said notice by filing a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed.
