The High Court held that the first respondent had no locus standi to file the writ petition and quashed the order of the Central Govern ment on the ground that the law reports published by it were not newspapers as defined in the Act and therefore the order made by the State Government on the basis of the recommendations of Justice Palekar was unsustainable. The appellant filed a Special Leave Petition before this Court against the said judgment of the High court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 The law reports which are being published by the Ist respondent are reports of recent decisions of the Supreme Court and of the high Courts in India which are public bodies and these are matters in which the public is interested. [778C] 1.2 In the instant case, the first Respondent has not been able to agree with the second respondent that the Law reports do not carry any news and that the public was not interested in them. The law report published by a Ist respondent contains information about the recent events which have taken place in the Supreme court or in the high courts which are Public bodies and those are matters of public importance. [779D] 1:3. In view of the fact that the expression 'newspaper ' as defined under the Act includes not merely `public news ' but also `comments on public news ', it is difficult to agree that the publication of the recent judgments itself is sufficient to make a law report a newspaper which may after some time cease to be a newspaper and become a book of reference. The Act in question is a beneficent legislation which is enacted for the purpose of improving the conditions of service of the employees of the newspaper establishments and hence even if it is possible to have two opinions on the construction of the provisions of the statute the one which advances the object of the legislation and is in favour of the employee for whose benefit the Act is passed has to be accepted. [780E F] 1 :4. The Law reports published in the law Reports of the Ist Respondent are newspapers and the employees employed by the first appellant in their production or publication of such law reports should be extended the benefit of the orders passed by the central Government on that basis.

The appellant was a licensee of the respondent. The respondent had been described as the licensee 's licensee and the recitals therein recite that the licensor was seized and possessed of and was otherwise well entitled as the monthly tenant of the workshop premises situated at 231, Ripon Road, Cooperative Building, Bombay being the premises in dispute. The appellant was described as a licensee '. The licence was renewed for a period of five years from 1st of September 1965 till 31st August, 1970. The licensor had agreed to allow the licensee to use and occupy the said premises for the purpose of carrying out his business of workshop for a further period of 5 years. The agreement was executed on 1st February 1973. The period of leave and licence was to commence from 1th of September, 1965 till 30th August, 1971. The licensee had agreed that the licensee would not terminate the said agreement earlier except on the ground of breach of any of the terms and conditions written therein. The license was to be effective from 1.9.1965. The suit premises were let out to the appellant on a monthly rent of Rs. 231/ per month. The plaintiff respondent filed an application for eviction under section 14(1)(e) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 on the grounds that the appellant was not a licensee and that he had been using the premises for carrying out its business of repair and maintenance. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the respondent was a tenant and not a tenant. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court held that the licence was not put an end to by the appellants and that in any event by filing the application for ejectment the appellant licensor had granted an implied licence to the respondent licensee to continue in possession till a decree of eviction was passed in his favour. The High Court also refused to interfere with the finding of the trial court that the defendant was a sub tenant. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In view of the intention of the parties in the document and the facts and circumstances of the case, it was a licence and not licence. good deal of submission was made before the High court that if it was not so, there was no estoppel. [21D] 1.2 The background of the facts of this case and the background of surrounding circumstances showed that the parties had agreed for leave and license between the parties to be renewed or any fresh agreement was entered into. It was a license and not an agreement. good dealing of submission made before this Court was a Licence and not lease. good deals of submission is a licence.

The appellant was the Ruler of a former State. The Ruler of that State, in exercise of his powers under article 295(2) of the Constitution, granted to him certain rights of ownership and possession of certain properties including lands belonging to the Ruler. In 1951, the Ruler promulgated an Ordinance called the Rajasthan Merged Territories (Administration of Property) Act, 1950, which was replaced by the Rajasthan Land Reforms Act, 1954. The Act provided for the continuance of laws in relation to the territories of the former State of Jodhpur and the provisions of the Act relating to the continuance and repeal of such laws were made applicable to the new State. In exercise of this power, the appellant was appointed Ruler of the erstwhile State of Rajasthan. On January 26, 1950 the Ruler passed an order under section 3(2)(a) of that Act declaring that the rights of the Ruler in relation thereto would be exercisable by him as a successor to the former Ruler. The appellant challenged the validity of this order on the grounds (1) that it was not competent to the State Government to make any law with respect to the rights conferred by the former ruler; (2) that the Ruler had no authority under article 294(2), and (3) that even if there was any liability of the latter State, the Act could not operate to confer any right on the appellant. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1 ) the Ruler having been recognised by the new sovereign as a Ruler under article 298(2); (2)(b) the Ruler continued to be an independent State till he passed any law repealing the old law which would affect the liability or even otherwise that law would prevail and the liability may disappear provided the new law is within the competence of the State legislature and does not transgress the constitutional limitations after the Constitution came into force; (3)(a), (b) and (c) were therefore invalid. HELD: (1)(a). The Ruler had been recognised as a sovereign by the old sovereign and was bound to act in his own name. [179 D] (b). The agreement was not a law. It was not an Act of State but it was a contract between the Ruler and the Ruler which was binding on him. [180 E F] (2). The appellant had been given the right to continue the laws, and as such he could not be allowed to take advantage of his position as a new sovereign. [181 G] (3). The State of Ajmer vs Ajmer Singh, ; , referred to. (4) The Ruler continued the old laws till they were altered or repealed by the fresh State law which was within the jurisdiction of the new Government and did not transgress its constitutional limitations.

The appellants were carrying on business in the State of Madras. They were assessed to sales tax for the year 1948 49 under the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939. The appellants contended that they had been using the goods as raw materials for manufacturing and selling their products and that the transactions were not liable to tax under section 14 of the Act. Held, that the appellants were not entitled to any deduction from the price or commodity in respect of commercial crops. The fact that the sales were effected by the appellants with the result that a person who is having a licence to trade in and about the place where the market is fixed, is deprived of his livelihood which is an unreasonable restriction upon his right to do business does not make him liable for payment of tax under the Act unless he pays the price of the commodity purchased at the time of the sale. The question whether a person is a dealer or not was one of fact and it was open to the State Government to decide in each case whether the transactions amounted to trade allowance. The object of section 14 was to provide for the better regulation of the business and to prevent evasion of tax by the dealers. The Act did not provide for any deduction of trade allowance from the prices or commodity agreed to be paid or transferred, it would be a trade allowance within the meaning of section 15 of the Madras Act. The contention that the provisions of the impugned Act were invalid because they contravened article 14 was rejected by this Court in Commissioner of Income tax vs M/s. D. N. Mukherjee & Co., ; , and the appellants had not produced any material to show that the said provisions were intended to be applied to them.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and sentenced to death on the ground that he had committed the murder of his wife. The High Court confirmed the sentence but reduced the sentences to transportation for life. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the High Court should have imposed a sentence of transportation for the offence of murder on the appellant and that the sentence should be reduced to transportation. HELD : (i) The High Courts were right in reducing the sentences of death to transportation in these two cases mainly because of the difference of opinion between the High Courts, not only on the question of guilt but also on the point of sentence. [426 B] (ii) The fact that the appellant was a young man and had no hand in the killing, and there was evidence that he did not give him any name would not make him guilty and so should be acquitted. [413 C D] (iii) The sentence of death imposed on the appel lant was excessive and it was not necessary to impose the lesser penalty. [414 E F] (iv) The appellant had been convicted by a Sessions Judge for murder on his own, but he did no more than inflict a comparatively light head injury. There was evidence to show that there was enmity between the accused and the deceased. It is true that the prosecution case was that the appellants were also there but it was difficult to believe that they would have joined in the attack and so had the actual murder been committed. But what the High court did was to reduce the sentences. [416 C D, F G] (v) The circumstances showed that the two accused were not present at the scene of the crime but were only a young brother and the tenant of the appellant in question. There is no reason why the sentence of imprisonment should be enhanced.

The petitioner was appointed as officiating Executive Engineer in Class I service but on 4.9.1965 he was reverted to the post of Assistant Engineer in officiating position and was reappointed on 4th September, 1965. He challenged that order by filing a writ petition before this Court contending that his reversion was illegal because he had not attained the age of 55 years by the date of the order and therefore on the date when he was compulsorily retired he was not entitled to draw salary and allowances which he would have been entitled to get in normal course. The petitioner contended that he was in Class II or Class II service or post and, therefore, on the dates of his compulsory retirement he had completed 55 years of age. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The purpose of Fundamental Rules 56(j)(i) is to confer power on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retire Government servant in the public interest and the classification of Government servants into two categories covered by sub clauses (i) and (ii) has a purpose behind it. If the officia tion is not brought to an end by reverting the Government servant to his substantive post before the power of compul sory retirement is exercised, the Government Servant must be taken to be in Class 1 or Class 11 service or Post at the relevant time and would come within the ambit of sub clause (i). [690G H] 1.2 The purpose for Fundamental Rules56(j) is not to confer powers on the Appropriate authority to compulsory retire Government servants in the Public interest and classification of government servants into three categories covered under sub clauses(i) & (ii), has a valid basis behind it, [691B C] 1:3. In the instant case, the petitioner was promoted as officiating Assistant Engineer which is a Class II post on 25.5.1971. He was reverted from the post to the said post when he had attained the maximum age of 50 years. The question whether a Government servant officiating in Class 11 or Class III service or a post can be retired compulsorily by exercising the power under Rule 56(1)(i), after he has attained the prescribed age of fifty five years, is not relevant to the exercise of power contained in F.R. 56(J) (i), because if the offici tion was not brought into an end either by reverting or reducing the Government servants, it would be open to the appropriate authori ty to compulsorily retired Government servant. [692C D] 1 :4. The possibility of a reversion to the substantive post is not germane to the exercising of power under F. R. 56 (j)(1).

The respondent Corporation issued a cheque for Rs. 1,00,000/ in favour of the appellant Corporation on 11th January 1961 and drawn on the State Bank of India, Bangalore. The cheque was encashed and the appellant had duly appropriated the amount and credited in the account towards the premium payable by the deceased. The appellant Corporation filed a suit against the respondent Corporation for recovery of the amount. The trial court decreed the suit holding that there was no concluded contract of insurance between the deceased and the Corporation and that the acceptance of the proposal was not binding on the Corporation. On appeal, the High Court held that the proposal must be accepted by the Divisional Manager and that only in this case the Corporation must be deemed to have waived by its conduct the formality, if any, of sending communication of its acceptance of proposal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Corporation that the policy was not a contract of Insurance and as such there was a concluded contract between the parties. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in coming to the conclusion that there is a concluded agreement of insurance. [354B] 2.1 The plea that Divisional Manager was the only authority to accept had not been specifically taken in the written statement filed on behalf the Corporation nor was it raised in the plaint. It was also not urged that the Corporation had waived by their conduct the formalities, ifany, of receiving the proposal. [355F G] 2(a) The plea of acceptance of insurance proposal and its acceptance must be considered as a defence to the suit. [356B C] 2b) The High court was in wrong in coming into the conclusion on the basis of the evidence and the averments made in the notice sent to the Corporation by the Life Insurance Corporation. [359C D] 3(a). The plea taken by the Corporation was not that the proposals were accepted by it. It is true that the letter dated 11th February 1961 was addressed to the Life Inspec tor, Bangalore but it was not proved that such a letter was sent by the corporation. The letter was addressed by the life Insurance Corporation to the Divisional Office of the Life Assis tration Corporation and was duly acknowledged by it in its accounts and the said letter was received by the respondent without any demur or objection. [358F G; 358A] 3.1 In the instant case, there is no concluded agreement between the Corporation as well as the Corporation to accept the proposal of the deceased, nor is there any evidence that such could have been the deposition in law. The plea raised by the Corpora tion was not accepted by both the courts below. [360B] 3:2. The respondent Corporation must therefore be deemed not to have condoned the delay in filing the suit and it must be presumed that the deceased had waived his right to claim the amount under the policy.

The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for recovery of certain amounts due from him on account of arrears of rent. The respondent contended that an order granting interim injunction was a final order and not a final one, and that the High Court had no jurisdiction to grant such an order. The trial court dismissed the application holding that the order granting injunction did not determine the rights of parties within the meaning of article 133 (1) (c). On appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The expression "final order" in section 205(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935 means an order which finally determines the points in dispute and brings the case to an end. [1055 C] (ii)The expression " final order" is not defined in the Code of Civil Procedure. It has been held by this Court that a final decision on the rights or liabilities of parties in dispute in a suit or proceeding is not final. The expression 'final order ' is not used in any technical sense, but in its popular sense, means a final adjudication by the court of the rights and obligations of the parties for determination in the suit or proceedings from which appeal has arisen. [1155 D] (iii)The word "final" in article 133(1)(c) means an interlocutory order passed in the exercise of the right to decide finally the rights, liabilities and obligations between the parties. The words "final orders" are not defined by the Code. They are intended to include all interlocutory orders which are final. [1255 E] (iv)The words " final orders" in Article 133(2) do not mean an order passed by the High court which finally decides the rights. It is only when a final determination on the right of the party in dispute takes place that the final decision is final. If the final determination is final, it cannot be said to be final. In the present case, the final adjudication was made and the plaintiffs may have to seek amendment of the plaint to get effective relief. [1355 F G] (v)The order refusing to grant an interim injunction did determine the right or obligations of parties. If it did not and the suit was a live one, yet to be tried, the order was held not to be a final decree within the definition of article 134(1).

The respondent assessee, a manufacturer of cotton fabrics, filed price lists in respect of the goods manufactured by it. The price at which he was selling the processed fabric would be the value of the grey cloth plus the value thereof and the manufacturing profit and expenses for the processing be Rs.5,000/ . The Assistant Collector of Central Excise rejected the claim on the ground that the assessee had failed to prove that the goods were not sold by him but only by way of job work done on job work basis. The Appellate Authority confirmed the order of the Assistant Collector. In revision, the Tribunal held that the assessable value of processed fabric was the value for the purpose of excise duty and therefore the value would be taken by the Excise authorities as the assessable valuation of the processed fabrics. The Revenue filed an appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The assessable value is the value on the basis of the job work performed by the assessee plus the manufacturing profits but not any other subsequent profit or expenses. It is necessary to include the processor 's expenses, costs and charges plus profit, but it is not necessary to included the trader 's profits who gets the fabrics processed because those would be post manufacturing profits. [346C D] 1.2 The assessable valuation is the price at the factory gate or deemed to be the price on the date of the sale of the manufactured goods. It may be that the market rate for the processed cloth would be higher than the prevailing market rate in respect thereof but it may not be necessary to add the trader to the cost of the processing. [347D] 1:3. The assessablevalue is the actual price at or about the date on which the manufactured fabric would have been sold by the processor plus the profit. But it is a matter of fact that the process of manufacture would have taken place in the factory and not in the market. It would be an error in applying the principle of valuation to the facts of the case. [345E] 1 :4. The value at which the processed cotton or man made fabric to the processor for processing on job worked basis would give a declaration to the manufacturer as to what would be his price at that point of time, and not any subsequent profit and expense. It was not necessary for the other assessee to include a trader ' profits who got the fabrics processing, because those will be postmanufacturing profits. The cost of packing the processed goods would be added only in the price of the process done plus manufacturing profit. [344F G] 1 5. The market rate of the cloth in the hands of the processor and the excise duty would be charged to the fabric on that basis provided that the declaration as to the price is at the time of the selling of the product, plus the profits. But the cost is not a part of the price for the job worked out by the manufacturer plus the cost.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti, Loharu. He was confirmed in that post in course of time. On January 21, 1974 he was promoted as a Head Clerk. The Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zilla Parishads (Haryana Amendment) Act, 1973 introduced extensive amendments in the Act of 1961. Section 33 of the Amending Act provided that persons employed by a Panchayat Samiti before April 1, 1973 and who were in service at the commencement of the amending Act shall continue to be governed on the same terms and conditions on which they were employed by the Panchayats Samiti from time to time. The appellant was confirmed as a head clerk on an ad hoc basis. On March 14, 1975 he was appointed a Head clerk. He continued to work as a full time Head Clerk till June 13, 1973 when the Amending Ordinance came into force. He challenged his absorption on a higher post in the Panchayat Samitis before the High Court of Punjab and Haryana. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant was entitled to continue in the service of the Panchayat even though he had been appointed as head clerk. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The appointment of the appellant to the post of a Head Clerks prior to his absorption in Government service had to be recognised and protected, despite the fact that such appointment was made after June 13 1973 when Amending Act came into effect. [738C] 1.2 In view of this deletion, the Panchayat Samities were divested of their power to make appointments to the Panchayat. The fact that the appel lant was promoted on an Ad hoc basis in January 1974 or the further fact that he was appointment lawfully to the posts of a head Clerk prior to the amendment came into operation on June 13. 1973 when amending Act came in force, cannot improve his position for the simple reason that these appointments were made after July 13,1973 when the Amendment Act came to be passed. [750D E] 1:3. The appointment was not made after the date on which the Panchayat had lost its power to making appointments to Panchayat. It could not, therefore, have appointed the appellant as a Sub Clerk in any event.

The appellants filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute belonged to the Math Sauna or the deity. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the Amauli properties were owned by the Math and therefore, the claim was not admissible under section 3(1) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms Act, 1950. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that: (i) The property in question belonged to a Math Saunakar who had installed a temple in the village Sauna and was therefore entitled as Sarbarakar to all the properties recorded in the deity 's name; (ii) the Amaulkar Yati was not a regularly constituted Mahant of Math Saiva and that the income from the property was liable to be assessed to tax. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The fund from which the Amauri properties were acquired constituted the personal property of Mahant Shivshankar Yati. [663 B] (2) The funds from which a Amauli property was acquired constituted an individual who had been appointed as Mahant of the Math. The income from these properties was transferred by Mahant Shivram Yati to his own predecessor in interest and not to the deity, and therefore the claim for exemption from the levy was made. [664 C] (3) The High Court was right in holding that the fund from whom the Amari properties were purchased constituted the Personal property of the Mahant Shiv Ram. [665 D] (4) The Fund from which income tax was collected by the appellant was a personal property and therefore a claim to exemption from levy was not made. The High court was right, in holding otherwise.

The appellants were displaced persons from West Pakistan. The Custodian General, by an order dated October 31, 1952, sanctioned the allotment of 24 standard acres and 5 1/4 units in favour of the respondents. On March 24, 1955, the Custodian General issued a notification under section 12(1) of the , directing that the allotment made to displaced persons be cancelled on certain specified grounds. The appellants challenged the validity of this order by means of a writ petition before the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the notification dated March 24 1955, issued under section 13(1), of the Act, was invalid as it was not in conformity with the provisions of sections 12 and 19 of the . (ii) the order of cancellation was bad because the Custodian had no power to cancel the allotment. HELD : (i)(a) The order of the Custodian dated October 30, 1952 was not a valid order under section 19(1). The order was therefore invalid. (b) The notification dated April 24, 1956, issued by the Central Government under section 10 of the was invalid because it was made in contravention of the provisions contained in sections 12(2), and 19(3) of Act No. XXXVII of 1954. [333 B C] (c) The Custodian had not taken any action against the appellants for cancellation of allotment. The order dated April 25, 1956 was therefore bad. [334 E F] (d) The effect of section 19 of Act XXXVII is that the displaced person to whom land was allotted "held" the land and was in possession of such property at the date of the notification. Therefore, it cannot be said that section 19 (1) was completely in conflict with section 10 Of the Act. [332 F G] (e) The provisions of section 12 and 13 of the are not inconsistent with those of sections 14 and 19. Section 19(2) is a provision which is in conflict between the provisions relating to acquisition of land and the provisions regarding compensation for the property acquired. It is implicit in this section that the evacuee person to whose allotment was allotted 'held ' the land, and was In possession of the property at that time, at the time of the acquisition, had become an evacuee property. [336 G H] (f) The words "in any case" in section 19 are wide enough to include cases where a displaced person is allotted land or land in excess of the compensation payable under the Act and forms part of the Compensation pool. The expression "allotted land" in the section means all land held by a person whether such allotment or lease was granted before or after the commencement of the act. [340 G H; 341 A] (g) The word "allot" is not defined in the Act but has been used in the sense in which it occurs in the , and the context in which the words are used, would indicate that the expression "in respect of any land" means all lands held by an evacuee or a person who was entitled to hold them immediately before the date on which the notification under s.12(1)(c) of .

The Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission invited applications from eligible candidates for recruitment to the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Women), District Inspectress of Girls Schools/Associate Regional Controllers of Girls School in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale (Care) and DistrictHOK of Girls schools/Associates Regional Controllers, in Uttar pradesh. The advertisement inviting applications from qualified candidates was published on May 5, 1985 and a corrigendum was published by the State Government on June 8, 1985. The recruitment examination was in two stages written and interview/personality test. After the written examina tion was over, on the basis of the results thereof success ful candidates upto a base limit have to be called to be interviewed. On account of improper feeding into the comput er some of the candidates who had better performance in the written examination were not called and candidates securing lesser marks in the viva voce were not only called for interview but were also finally selected. When this position was known and upon an inquiry was factually estab lished, the Public Service Com mission cancelled the entire recruitment examination and asked for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the ground that they had better performances in the selection process. The High Court upheld the action of the Public Services Commission and dismissed the writ petitions. Hence these appeals by special leave. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 When no defect was pointed out in regard to the written test and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the oral examination from the interview, there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the recruitment examina tions. [125B] 1.2 The situation could have been appropriately met by setting aside the recruitment and asking for a new interview of the two Scheduled Caste candidates and five Backward Class candidates has become final and would not be disturbed. The State Public Service commission should have been more careful in dealing with the matter so that four years in the process of recruitment would not have been lost and the public cause would not hail if the litigation could have reached. [126C D] 1:3 In the instant case, when no defect had been pointed out by the appellant, the High Court has upheld the actions of the public Service Commission and has dismissed the Writ Petitions. The selection of two Scheduled Castes candidates and 5 Backward Class candidate has become complete and would be in accordance with the interview part of recruitment and on the principle of equality of opportunity enshrined in Article 14 of the Constitution. [127F G] 1 :4 In the process, there is hardly any justification for cancellation of the written parts of the selection examina ble. The procedure adopted by the Public Commission has been completely misconceived and has resulted in violation of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitu tion. [128B C] 2.1 The situation can have been suitably met by set aside the selection and asking the for a second interview of only eligible candidates in accordance wit h the written and the freshly held interview became eligible for selection. There is no justification to cancel the written Part of the Recruitment Examination and asking a fresh examination of all other eligible candidates. [129C D, E] 2:2 The State Government should have be more careful while dealing with matters so that 4 years in process of selection would not has been lost.

The appellant, who was the owner of a house in which his wife was residing, filed a suit for recovery of possession of the said house and properties. The respondent contended that the appellant had no knowledge about the date of death of the deceased and held that the appeal had abated and that there was no ground for setting aside the abatement. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decree holding that after the death of Som Dass, Shiam Dass as his legal representative could not be made a party to the suit. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the properties belonged to the Dera and he was the lawfully appointed mahant of the Dwara, the appeal could not continue under Q.10(1) in view of the fact that the period of limitation for impleading them had expired. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court should have granted leave to the appellant to prosecute the appeal. [488B] 2.1 In order to bring an end to a suit, the suit may be continued by or against the person who has filed it and as it was in a representative capacity that the suit was instituted and as such the appeal can be continued under Q 10(1). The fact that it was after Som Dass died that Shiam Das was elected to be the Mahant of the dera, could make no difference when there was a certainty as to the person whom would be elected to fill their place. [490C D] 22 In the instant case, the appellant was sued in his capacity as a person who claimed (though illegally according to the respondent) as mahant from the date on which the suit had been instituted and the appeal came to an end. The suit was filed on the basis that the appel lant as the lawfully constituted mahant was entitled to manage the properties of theDera and the properties appertaining thereto by the appellant purporting to be his successor. [495F G] 23 In the present case, there is no doubt that the property belonged to Dera. The appellant was suing in his own capacity and there was devolution of interest during the pendency of the suit and the suit could not have continued under the Q. 10( 1) in any sense because the period for limitation for an application to impleaded them under Order 22, rule 10 had elapsed. [492A B] 24 In the circumstances of the case, it is clear that devolution of the interest in the subject matter of the appeal took place when Shiamdas was elected as mahants of the office of mahant subsequent to the death and the appellant could be added as parties under Order 23, rule 3 or 4.

The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board. They were promoted to the post of Superintending Engineer, and were later promoted to officiate as Superintending Engineer. The Government of Andhra Pradesh issued a notification dated October 29, 1979 amending the Fundamental Rules by adding clause (2) to Article 309 of the Constitution. The petitioners challenged the validity of the amendment on the ground that it was violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitu tion. The High Court dismissed their writ petitions. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the amendment of February 17, 1983 to the Fundamental Rule was not applicable to them as they had been issued by the Government of India in exercise of its power under Article 309 read with Article 313 of the constitution and therefore the amendment was bad for a total non application of mind to the relevant facts and circumstances bearing on the question of fixation of retirement. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The amendment of March 19, 1983 by adding cl. (2), to clause (1) of Article 309, is not violative of Article 14 or Article 16 because it is not arbitrary or unreasonable in the circumstances of the case. [475E] 2. The object of the Fundamental rules is to provide for a uniform and uniform treatment between persons belonging to different categories and to provide that persons similarly situated should be treated alike. It is not possible to lay down any general principle which would govern the interpretation of statutes. [476G H] 3. The power of the Government to alter or amend the conditions of service of its employees cannot be questioned on the grounds of arbitrariness or unreasonableness. [477A B] 4. The Fundamental Rules are intended to have a salutary effect on the creation of incentives to the deserving employees, and that the general trend was for reducing the age of retirement from 55 to 58 years in the instant case. It was not arbitrary nor unreasonable in any manner. [478D E] 5.

The Haryana Sales Tax Act, 1973 was enacted to provide for the levy of tax on purchase of goods in the State. Section 9(1) provides that where a dealer liable to pay tax under this Act, fails to pay the tax payable by him under section 9, he shall be levied, subject to the provisions of section 17, a tax on the purchase value of such goods at such rate as may be notified under section 15. The Haryana Sales tax Act 1973 was amended by Haryana Act 20 of 1988 with retrospective effect from 9.4.1979. The amendment made in 1986 provided that the purchase price of raw materials when sold by a dealer shall not exceed the maximum rate fixed by the Government under section 5(3) of the Act. The appellants, who were dealers in cement, were registered as dealers under the Haryana Sales Act, 1972. They filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the amendment made by the Amendment Act. A Division Bench of the High court allowed the writ petitions and quashed the amended provisions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that section 9(i) of Haryana Sales Taxation Act 1973 did not impose a tax at all as the goods were sold in the course of inter State trade or commerce or in the way of export out of the territory of India within the meaning of section 5 (3) and therefore, the amendment was not applicable to them. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The effect of the decision is that the words "or despatches the manufactured goods to a place outside the State in any manner otherwise than by way of sale in the territory" in section 5 of the C.S.T. Act, 1956, are not attracted to the facts of the present case. [351B] 2. The object of the Haryana Act is to provide that the tax on purchases should be levied at a rate which may be specified by the State Government under Section 9 of the Central Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1988. This definition includes within the definition of "turnover" the purchase cost of goods liable to tax under section 4 but, the goods presently in question are not sold as such. [352C] 3. The words "in the course or in relation to the inter State sale" occurring in Section 9 (1) of C.P.T., 1973 are wide enough to include cases where the manufactured articles are disposed of only by way or through a dealer and used them in the manufacture of goods for the purpose of (a) local sale; (b) inter State sales; or (c) sale in course of export outside the territory. [353D] 4. The definition of 'turnover ' includes within it, any sum which is payable by a registered dealer under section 3(1)(b). The words 'in the case of goods sold ' are wide and include all kinds of sales including those specified in Schedule B to the Act, which are not covered by the definition. [354E] 5. The expression "turnover ' means the aggregate amount of sale price paid or payable in cash or in kind but does not include any other sum charged by a person for anything done or omitted to be done in the execution of a contract. [355F] 6. The word "turnover " is used in the sense of "sale" and not as "purchase value". [356G] 7. The term "turnover", in section 9 (i) means the total amount of purchase price paid by a purchaser to a registered person for the sale or purchase of any goods, whether as principal or otherwise. [356H] 8. The Legislature has used the expression "sale price" in the definition clause and not the words 'purchase value of goods '. The legislature has used that expression in the Act with reference to which it is made. It does not use the word "sale". [355G H] 9.

The appellant was a registered dealer under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1948. He sold his goods to the respondent who in turn sold them to the appellant. The respondent filed a return of sales tax on the ground that the sales were not their property till they crossed the customs barrier and thus entered the export stream. The Sales Tax Officer held that the goods remained the sellers ' property till the goods had been brought and loaded on board the ship and so the sales could be exempted from tax under article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution. The appellant appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who dismissed the appeal holding that the transactions were not liable to purchase tax under section 10(b). On further appeal, the High Court held that there was no circumstance which would justify a conclusion that the parties came to a special agreement that though the sales had been oncart track property in the goods would pass to the buyer at some point of time before shipment. Held, that the words " a person " in section 10 (b) are wide enough to include a registered person and the purchasing dealer does not show to the satisfaction of the Collector that the articles have been despatched by him or by a person to whom he has sold the goods. The words " the person who has given such certificate" in section 8(b) mean "a registered dealer to whom the certificate has sold it". The words 'the person who is not a registereddealer ' are wide and they do not include a person who does not have any special agreement with the purchasing dealers that the article should be despatched by a registered dealers. The word " registered dealer" in the section means a registered under the Act. The expression "a Registered dealer" has been defined in section 2(g) of that Act to mean a registered registered dealer. The definition of " registered dealers" is wide enough and it includes a person whose name is not registered. The fact that the certificate is issued by the purchasingdealer does not make any difference. The certificate is only a registered one and the purchase is made by a Registered dealer.

The appellant, who was a married woman, filed an application under section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code 1973 for a monthly allowance for maintenance. The Magistrate found that the appellant had transferred the suit premises to the respondent and also the shares of the Cooperative Housing Society which built the flat concerned. The appellant 's appeal against the order of the Magistrate was dismissed by the Sessions Judge. In an appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Courts below had overlooked the plain provision in the Explanation (b) to section 125(1) of the Code and that there must be proof of neglect to maintain to attract s.125 and his third contention was that there should be proof that the respondent was a divorcee within the cognisance of that provision. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The main purpose of the payment under any customary or personal law is to avoid destitution of the divorcee and to provide her with wherewithal to maintain herself. [81 C] 2. The object of the Payment of mehar money, as a customary discharge, is to ensure that the wife does not get remarried. The whole scheme of section 127(3)(b) is manifestly to recognise the substitute maintenance arrangement by lump sum payment organised by the custom of the community or the personal law of the parties. [82 D] 3. The purpose of payment under a customary or Personal Law must be to obviate destitution, of the Divorcee and the obligor, not pro tanto but wholly. The intention of the legislature is clear that every divorce otherwise eligible for the benefit of maintenance should be made out if the hurdle of section 125 (4) is to be over come. [83 E] 4. The expression "withal" in the proviso to s. 125(3) of Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 has no application where the husband, by customary payment at the time of divorce, has adequately provided for the divorce, a subsequent series of recurrent does is contra indicated and the husband liberated. [84 E] 5. The conclusion that the liability to pay maintenance had ceased on account of the payments of the sum stipulated by customary or family law whose quantum is more or less sufficient to do duty for maintenance allowance is correct.

The appellant was a bidder for the contract of supply of rice. The Collector of the district after perusal of the office note passed order on 25th March, 1988 which is produced in verbatim below: "No notice has been given to the appellant of the proposal of black listing the appellant. " The order dated 25th April, 1988 was passed pursuant to the order of the Collector. The letter dated 25.3.1988 states as follows: "The Collector of District after perusal, of the said office note pass order on the said representation of the appellant." The letter further states that no notice had been given by the appellant to the appel lant of the proposed black listing. The appellant challenged the aforesaid order before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The last portion of the order in so far as it directs black listing of the appellan tant in respect of future contracts cannot be sustained in law. In that view of the matter, the last portion is not affected. [868C] 1.2 The last part of the Order in so much as it relates to the cancellation of the bid of the bidder is set aside. So far as the cancellation is concerned, that is not a ground for quashing the order. In this view of matter, there is no question of any violation of principles of natural justice. [886D] 1:3. The last paragraph of the aforesaid Order in respect to it directs that the appellant be placed in the black list in respect in respect thereof in respect o.a. 11,900 (Rupees eleven thousands only) per month Dak in an auction held on 27.3,1988 and he as given the shop of Beni Country liquor but after signing in Bandobasti Register he did not deposit dak amount. [ 868E] 1 :4. The order will, however, not prevent the State Government or the appropriate authorities from taking any future steps forIBa tion for blacklisting the appellant if the Government is so entitled to do so in accordance with law indicating the reasons therefor.

The appellant was the landlord of a house in Madras. The respondent landlord filed an application under section 4 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 for fixation of fair rent in respect of the premises leased to him. The Rent Controller rejected the application on the ground that the subject matter of the lease was only a vacant site and not a vacant land. On appeal, the High Court held that the Rent Controller had no jurisdiction to fix the fair rent under section 64 C which was applicable only to the vacant site. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant tenant that since the subject Matter of the leased property originally formed part of an extent of land and the Rent Control Act was not applicable, the Rent controller had no juris diction to fix such fair rent. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The question whether a landlord is a tenant in or landlord of, the building and (2) what the fair rental of the property should be in accordance with the provisions of the Act is only a determination as to the fair or standard rent for the premises. [550G] 1.2 In view of the finding that the lease in question was only an vacant site, the question on which the jurisdiction of the Rent control ler under the Act was excluded is only the determination as regards the fair and standard rent of the building. If the Rent Authority did not decide that question properly, the matter would have to be raised in appeal to the Court of Small Causes and would give this Court no jurisdiction. [552B C] 1:3. The question on the question whether the order in the earlier rent control proceedings decided to the contrary and fixing the fair standard rent is null and void or merely one that is valid until set aside, the answer has to turn on the true nature and scope of the jurisdiction conferred on the Rent Court under the Tamil nadu Act. [553C D] 1 :4. The terms of section 64 of the Madras Buildings (lease and Rent) Control)Act, 1960 are not decisive on the point of ouster of the civil court 's jurisdiction. If, and only if, this relationship exists between the parties, the rent Controller steps in for a limited purpose to determine what the proper rent is and then fades out of picture. In such a case, the tenant would be entitled to recover the rent from the tenants, it will have to pass a decree in favour of the landlord on the basis of the fair rents fixed by the Rent Act. If and only when this relationship existed between the par ties, the landlord steps in seeking eviction of the tenant on the strength of the valid lease deed. [554D E] 1 5. The Court has to decide whether the applicant is a 'tenant ' or not. If it does not decide the question properly so, the decision will be final and binding.

The petitioner was a candidate for the post of Veterinary Officer in the Mysore State. He was selected and appointed as Veterinary Officer on an integrated seniority list. The respondent, who was a party to the writ petition, challenged the validity of the order of his appointment on the ground that he had been denied due opportunity to object to the proposed assign ment of a place to him in the seniority list although he was given due opportunity. The High Court held that the petitioner 's claim against the final list was premature as the final seniority list was still to be prepared after hearing objections. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the final gradation list since the petitioner had not been heard before the final lists were prepared. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Courts have rightly held that a person whose seniority is to be determined under section 115 of the , must be given an opportunity to make a representation with regard to the two points urged by him and if he was to object, he should have a further opportunity against even a final seniority lists. [828 D] (2) The petitioner ' s claim against final list though he was not heard before it was finalised, was not justified. [829 E F] (3) The principle recognised in Shankariah 's case is not applicable to such cases. If the Central Government has acted properly according to the provisions of the Act, it is open to it to give a person affected an opportunity of putting forward his objections before final list is prepared. But once he has had that opportunity, it cannot possibly be said that he should not have a second opportunity against all the final stages of the list. [827 E F; 828 A B] (4) The respondents were entitled to an opportunity for making a representation in respect of two points raised by them before the High Courts.

The petitioners, a partnership firm carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and export of cut and polished diamonds, were granted Additional licences for the period of 12 months and they were required to pay excise duty on the value of the goods imported. The petitioners filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the validity of the said licences. This Court dismissed the petitions holding that the petitioners had been granted Additional Licences under the Import & Export Policy 1978 79 and the Export Houses, like the petitioners, who were granted additional licences on or after April 1, 1988, on the basis of exports made during 1986 87 or earlier periods have been denied the facilities which have been given to Export Houses who were issued Additional licences on the ground that they had been denied facilities which had been given by them to Export House. The Court also held that under Import & Exports Policy 1978 80 additional licences were to be given on the same terms and conditions as in the Import and Export Policy 1988 91, and that the Export House could not be granted any additional licence for the diamonds components and consumables covered by Appendices 3 and Part A of the Import Policy 198891. The writ petitions filed by the petitioners challenging the constitutional validity of sub para (10) of para 218 of the Imports & Exports (Control) Order, 1985 were dismissed by this Court on May 5, 1986. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that there is no similarity between the petitioners who have been granted additional licence on the one hand and Export Houses which are granted Additional Licence under the import and Export policy for the subsequent years and since there has been relaxation in the matter of policy of canalisation of imports under sub para 215 in respect of Additional licences granted to Export houses under the Imports and Exports Policy 1988 92, the petitioners are also entitled to a similar relaxation. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The licences issued to the petitioners were valid for a period of twelve months and the said period has expired during the pendency of these writ petitions. [236C] 2. Under Import & export policy 1978 79 Additional Licences were to he given on "as isner in the Policy for the year 1978 79" and those who are granted additional licenses under the Export and Import Policy for that year would be entitled to import the goods which can be so imported under the prevailing Import Policy. The period of validity of such licences should be extended so that the Petitioners can avail the same and are able to import, import the same. [237D] 3. Under the Import Trade Control Policy 197879 Additional Licences are to be granted on the "as wasner in Policy for exportation under sub Para (4) of paragraph 215 in the case of Export Houses". The petitioners who were given additional licences under the said Import & Import Policy 197880 have to be treated at par with Export Houses. [238E] 4. Under import and export policy of 1978 79 the basis for grant of Additional Licences is the f.o.b. value of exports. The licence issued to them has been valid for the said year and since no additional licences have been issued for a much lesser value under the original order, they are also not entitled to any additional concession. The appellant assessee is a manufacturer of drums and containers. The assessee supplied drums to the buyers in packed condition and the containers were not returnable by the buyer, there fore, the value had to be included in the assessable value. The Department took the view that at the time of removal the goods were delivered from the factory in packed conditions and the container was not returnable to by the buyers, there being no packing material for the manufacture of drums, the cost of packing could be included as part of the assessable price. The appellant assessee filed appeals before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who held that at all relevant times the cost was the "value" of the containers and not the value, and hence, the valuation had to he included in its assessable value under section 4(4)(d)(i) of the Act. The Tribunal allowed the appeals preferred by the assessee and held that the cost for packing could only be included when the packing is either manufactured by the manufacturer or purchased by the asses see. In the appeal before this Court, on behalf of the Revenue it was contended that since at the relevant time the goods are delivered from factory in pack condition and containers were no returnable to the assessee, the price had to include in the value of such goods only when the packed is sold at the factory gate. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1.1 The object and purpose of the levy, the meaning of the expression "assessable value" as interpreted in section before its amendment cou pled with the now well established position that the amend ment intended to make no change in this position, the use of the word "cost" rather than "value", the nature of the other payments referred to in sub clause (ii) all these show beyond doubt that while generally the normal price for which the goods is sold in packed Condition and the packing was not delivered by the seller to the buyer to the manufacturer, in all other cases the cost is to be added to the price except where the packing has been of a durable nature and returnable to, the manufacturer.

The trial court accepted the prosecution evidence and convicted the accused under section 4(1) readwith section 5 of the Act and under sections 161 I P.C., and under Section 5(1)(a) read along with section 6(1). On appeal, the High Court acquitted the appellant on the ground that there was no independent evidence regarding the demand, the messenger who had contacted PW 1 at the behest of the appellant had not been examined. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The prosecution has failed to prove the guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The conviction cannot therefore be sustained. C. and section 5 1(a) of Prevention of Corpo ration Act, is to be maintained, no separate sentence need be award ed under section161 I.p.C.[340D] (4) The High Court thought that though PW 1 had returned the loan and that he was given the money for the Dipawali, it could not be said that there had been consistent explanation for the appe lant 's. (5) The conviction under Section 161 I .P. C., and section 4 (2), read with Section 5 (I)(d), of the prevention of Corruption act are not sustainable. [343G H] (6) The accused had even by preponderance of probability succeeded in rebutting the presumption arising under section4(1 ) of the Criminal Law Act which has not been rebutted.

The appellant temple was founded by a public trust known as 'Gandhi '. The deity installed a temple in the name of Sakharam Maharaj at Amalner. The temple was managed by a committee appointed by the Government and the temple was taken over by the State Government under section 3(1) of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950. The appellant claimed that the Sansthan was a private property and not a public religious trust. The Charity Commissioner held that the temple had been dedicated to the deity for the benefit of the Hindu public as a whole and not as a public institution. The High Court on appeal by special leave granted certificate under article 133(1)(c) of Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The endowment was in favour of the idol itself and the property had always been treated as trust property even by the Commissioner. [538 C] (ii) The temple is a public temple within the meaning of section 2(13) of Bombay Public Trust Act, 1951. It is a private one and not an institution. [525 D E] (iii) The dedication to the public or the worship of the deity was in the nature of a trust property but it was a public endowment. [500 G] (iv) The High court was right in holding that the endowment was a Public Trust within the definition of section 3 of the Act. [511 C D] (v) The appellant had not been able to prove that the deity installed in the temple is an ancient temple or a private institution. It was also not proved that the idol installed in any temple was ever treated as a trust.

The petitioner was arrested and detained in execution of a warrant issued under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876. The petitioner challenged his arrest on the ground that section 46(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, infringed article 14 of the Constitution as it contravened article 21 of the constitution. Held, that section 45(2), which provides for two different and alternative methods of recovery of arrears of land revenue, provided for two distinct and alternative modes of recovery, namely, (1) by attachment and sale of property belonging to the petitioner, and (2) by detention in execution thereof, are not unconstitutional under article 14. The provisions of section 46 (2), as they stood at the time when the Act was passed, were intended to be read into section 46 and therefore, if there be any vice of discrimination in the State laws that vice cannot but be regarded as having crept into section 45 (2). The word " arrear" in section 46 is not used in a sense which is capable of being understood in its ordinary sense. It is used in the widest possible terms to include arrears of rent and other dues recoverable from an assessee under a decree. The expression " arrears of revenue" in the context means arrears of income tax, and does not mean arrears of interest or other dues which are recoverable from the assessee under any decree. In the present case, the petitioner was already arrested and is being detained in jail for a longer period of time. The State laws prescribe the procedure for recovery of dues and clothes the Collector with the power to apply either of the two methods, that is to say, he may issue a warrant of arrest under section13 of the Act.

The respondents were the owners of a Port Trust, which was established under the Bombay Port Trust Act, 1948. The Trustees of the Port Trust were appointed by the Central Government under section 3(1) of the Act and they were paid overtime wages for overtime work in accordance with the provisions of the Bombay Dock Workers ' Union Rules, 1949. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said rules on the ground that they contravened the provisions contained in sections 13 and 14 of the , as they had not been given an opportunity to show cause against the proposed action. The High Court held that the Act was applicable only to the employees of the respondent Port Trust and not to the respondents. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The Trustees were entitled to three hours ' overtime if required to work beyond 12 hours. The provisions of section 13 of the are mandatory and they must be complied with before an employee can claim overtime wages. [912 E] (ii) The Act and the Rules fix the number of hours of work in a six day week. The maximum number of times of work is fixed under this Act by the time the workman is either made to work or the interval is not specified. The period of work of an adult worker in a factory shall be so arranged that inclusive of his intervals for rest under section 55 they shall not spread over more than ten and a half hours in any day. [936 G H] (iii) The provisions contained therein are mandatory. The Act does not provide for the maximum number or hours of overtime. It is for this reason that a variable recess is in force at the Prince 's and Victoria Docks and due notice of the interval was given by specifying a day in advance the hours of rest. [981 A B] (iv) The workers at the time of the work are not entitled to any wages. They are paid overtime for overtime. The workers are entitled to overtime wages if required under the provisions Of section 13.

The appellant was the tenant of a shop in the premises in question. The respondent landlord filed a suit for ejectment against the appellant on the ground that he had let out the shop to the appellant after the expiry of 10 years from October 1, 1976. The appellant pleaded that apart from the controversy about the date when the suit was filed, there were no other issues framed and therefore the trial court passed a decree for eviction. The Trial Court decreed the suit on the basis of the pleadings of the parties and dismissed the suit. The High Court in second appeal reversed the judgment of the Trial Court and decreed the plaintiff 's suit for eviction on the grounds that (i) the landlord had failed to prove that he was entitled to protection under Section 20(2) of the Act; (ii) the tenant had not been given notice of termination of tenancy before terminating his tenancy; and (iii) the appellant tenant had failed in proving that he has been in possession of the shop for a period of 10 year. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since during the pendency of the proceedings in this Court 10 years have elapsed even if the date of completion is taken to be 1.10.1976, the appellant cannot be said to have been in continuous possession of any shop for more than 10 years and therefore a decree of eviction could only be passed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court was right in holding that the suit filed by the landlord was not maintainable because (i ) the tenant has failed to establish that he is entitled to the protection under the Act and (ii). (iii ) The appellant tenant will be entitled to protect his possession from eviction if he fails to prove his case. [167D] 1.2 In order to attract section 20(1) of East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, the landlord must establish that the tenant is in actual possession of a building for more then 10 years. The tenant has to prove affirmatively that he does not have any other suitable residential accommodation. He must also prove affirmative and negatively that the landlord has failed in establishing that he will be able to pay rent for the period of ten years. [168E F] 1:3. In order that a decree may be passed, it is necessary that the plaintiff should show that he bona fide requires the premises for his own occupation or use and occupation. The requirement must be bona fide. It is not enough if the tenant does not pay rent to the landlord. He has to establish his case by leading evidence. [169F] 1 :4. In a suit filed on the date fixed for trial, the plaintiff must prove that the defendant was in actual or constructive possession of such building for a continuous period of more than ten years and he is not entitled to any relief under section 20 of the East Punjab Act. [170A B] 1 5.

The respondent was the thika tenant of a thika Tenancy. The appellant filed an application under section 3 of the West Bengal Thika Tenancy Act, 1949 for the eviction of the respondent on the ground that he had been in arrears of rent from 1st October 1952 to 31st March 1953 and that he was entitled to be ejected from the said land. The trial court held that the appellant had not proved that he ever made any application under s.3 of the Act for ejectment and dismissed the suit. On appeal, the High Court held that at the time when the appeal of the tenant was disposed of by the Subordinate Judge, the rights of the parties were governed by the Thika tenancy Act of 1949 and the definition of a ' thika tenants in that Act was not such as to afford any protection to the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the provisions of section 4 of the Calcutta Thika Tenants Act, 1948 were applicable only to cases where there was no dispute about the existence of one of the grounds specified in section 3 and therefore the definition did not afford any such protection to him; (ii) the words "any of the three grounds" occurring in section 4(2) of the said Act were wide enough to include all grounds which could be taken into consideration in the notice to quit in accordance with section 3, and (iii) the expression "any other ground" in section 5 of the Bengal Thikka Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1952, did not mean that the provisions contained in section 6 would apply to a case where there is no dispute regarding the existence or non compliance with the requirements of the section.

The High Court of Allahabad, Bench Secretaries were on a higher pay scale than that of Section Officers. The High Court directed that all Bench Secretaries may be given the same scale of pay which is being given to Superintendents or the Section Officers, as admissible to Section Officers in the pay scale of Rs.500 1,000 as recommended by the Pay Commission. The State Government has also been directed to say that the nomenclature of posts of 10 Bench Secretaries appearing in column 5 of the said table shall be Bench Secretaries Grade I and the nomenclature ' rest Bench Secretaries of equal pay scale will be Bench Secretary Grade II and the post of Bench Secretaries grade I and Grade II will be of the same duties and responsibilities. The appellant, a Senior Clerk in the High Court, was working as an Assistant Registrar in the Allahabad High Court. He was promoted to the post in the year 1973. In the seniority list prepared by the High court, he was shown at serial No. 1 whereas the appellant was shown as senior to the respondents. On the basis of the recommendations made by the Third Pay Commission, the pay scales recommended by it were revised and the pay structure recommended by that Committee was changed from Rs.400 750 to Rs. 400 750. The respondents filed a writ petition in the Lucknow High Court challenging the validity of the revised pay scale. The learned Single Judge allowed the petition holding that the recommendations of the Third Central Pay Commission were not binding on the appellant as no rules had been framed by him for the purpose of entitlement to higher pay scales. The Division Bench also held that the respondents were entitled to get the same scales of pay as was being given in the case of the appellant. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Courts should not have interfered with the recommendations and the rules framed by the Chief Justice of the High 'Court were violative of the constitutional right to equality enshrined in Article 14 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The High Courts are under a duty to consider whether the recommendations contained in the Rules are binding on all concerned or not. If it has a rational nexus with the object to be sought for, as reiterated before a certain amount of value judgment of the administrative authorities who are charged with fixing the pay Scales has to be left with them and it cannot be interfered with by the Court unless it is demonstrated that either it is irrational or based on no basis or arrived mala fide either in law or in fact. [297G H] 1.2 The principle of "equal pay for equal work" has to he construed in the first place. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value Judgment by those who are charge with the administration in fixing the scales of Pay and other conditions of service. If the Court has a reasonable nexus with object to being sought for the, as stated under the Rules, the classification made under the rules cannot be said to be violative of Article 14. [298A B] 1:3. The principle is that if the Court had a rational connection with the objects to be taken into consideration, as explained before a particular amount of valuation of the work done by the officers is differ. But the classification has to satisfy two tests: (i) whether there is any element of benefit or not; and (ii) whether the decision is based on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group. [300C D] 1 :4.

The Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 was enacted to provide for the establishment of a Municipal Corporation and for the purpose of taxation have powers which are municipal corporation or a municipal council has under the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 or the Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act. Section 127A of the Act provides that for the purposes of taxation, the Special Area Development Authority shall have the powers which a Municipal Council or a Municipal council has, as the case may be, under the M.P. Municipal Corporation Adhiniyam, 1956, or the Munici pal Area Development Authorities Act, 1957. The State Government by a notification dated April 1, 1976 exempted from the operation of section 127A the areas specified in the Schedule to the Act from the levy of property tax. The appellant Municipality challenged the validity of the said exemption on the ground that it was beyond the competence of the State Legislature to enact the impugned Act and that the provisions of the Madhya pradesh Municipalities Act were ultra vires the powers conferred by section 127 A of the Municipalities Act and the Municipal Corporation was not competent to impose the property tax without following the procedure prescribed by sections 129 and 133 of the Municipal Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Municipality that (i) the provisions contained in section 127B of the M .P. Municipalities Act or section 135 of the Corporation Act which were introduced by an amendment made after the enactment of section 69(d), could not be invoked for levying property tax, and (ii) the property taxes are imposed by respondent 1 under section 127C of the Municipality Act and section 135A of Municipal Corporation Acts. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High court was right in holding that the property Tax is imposed by the State legislature on the basis of the declaration contained in Section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1952. [22D] The power conferred by the said Act on the State Government to regulate and develop the Coal mines so as to ensure rational and scientific utilisation of coal resources is not in conflict with the power conferred under section 69 (d) of the , which provides that the properties tax shall not be leviable, inter alia, on "buildings and lands owned by or vesting in the Union Government". The State Legislature had no competence to pass a law on the subject. [23D E] The property tax is imposed under section 128A of a Municipalities Act for the benefit of persons who are residents of the area concerned. Section 128A(2) of that Act provides for the constitution of special areas, laying down by sub section (4) that the Municipal Commissioner shall have power to levy property tax in respect of buildings and lands acquired or requisitioned by the Union Govern ment. The power to impose property tax was conferred on the Government under section 126A of Municipalities Act which provides for a maximum period of five years from the date of commencement of the municipal Act, 1973. [24F G] The State of Madhya Pradesh vs Shri Om Prakash & Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellant was granted a lease of the land in dispute for a period exceeding one year. The lease was for a term exceeding one years and fell within the purview of section 20(1) of the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms Act, 1950. The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for a declaration that the lease was not enforceable against the Government. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant had no right to terminate the lease and that as the lease in question was for an period exceeding two years it was not executable against the government. On appeal, the High Court held that the termination of the lease by the Government was valid under section 20 (1) and that the Government could not be said to have terminated the lease. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The words "such right" in the third proviso to section 20 of the Act refer to the rights created after the 1st day of July 1945, for a further period of one year would also be valid and enforceable by the government against the person in whose favour such right had been created. [560 C] (i) The words 'such right ' in the second proviso relate to the right created after July 1, 1945, but after July I, 1945 for a certain period. The effect of the second Proviso is that rights created before the notified date but after 7th July, 1945 are liable to be avoided under the second provisos. [561 E] (ii) The third proviso applies only where the right has been created in any land or building and not where the lease is for a fixed period. It does not apply where the lessee has created a right in any other land or buildings and the rights of the Government are not affected by the second or the third provisos. The words, "such rights" in section 20 are wide enough to include those created after 7 1 1945, which were intended to be operative from July 1 1945.
